Plants are **producers**; animals are **consumers** (herbivores eat plants, carnivores eat other animals).

- Grass → insects → frog → snake → eagle
- Grass → deer → tiger

Many food chains link to form a **food web**. Each organism depends on others.

steps.title: Decomposers and humus
steps.body: Micro-organisms (bacteria, fungi) and small animals that convert dead plants and animals into a dark-coloured substance called **humus** are **decomposers**. Humus makes soil fertile and holds water. Dead leaves on the forest floor decompose quickly in warm, moist conditions.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Make a food chain with these: snake, grass, eagle, insect, frog. → **Grass → insect → frog → snake → eagle**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: What happens if all decomposers vanish?

A: Dead bodies and leaves would pile up, nutrients would not return to soil, and plants would not get enough nutrients.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting a food chain with an animal — it starts with a producer (plant).
- Thinking decomposers are harmful — they recycle nutrients.

activity.prompt: Arrange the food chain.

quiz.why: Plants are producers, as they make food from sunlight. So every food chain begins with them, and herbivores and carnivores come after.
Humus is the dark, fertile substance formed when decomposers break down dead plants and animals.
Fungi and bacteria are decomposers. They break down dead plants and animals into simpler substances.
A deer feeds on plants, so it is a herbivore. A carnivore eats other animals.

quiz.q: Many interlinked food chains form a
quiz.why: Many food chains linked together in a forest form a food web.

lessons.title: Forests as green lungs: air, rain and soil

scenes.text: In a village near a forest, the river runs clear even in monsoon.
Downstream, where the forest was cut, the river turns muddy and floods.
Tree roots hold the soil; forests also help bring rain.

steps.title: Green lungs
steps.body: Plants release **oxygen** in photosynthesis and use **carbon dioxide**. Animals and plants use oxygen for respiration. Forests help **maintain the balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide** in the air, so they are called **green lungs**.

steps.title: Rain and climate
steps.body: Trees release water vapour by **transpiration**, which helps form clouds and bring **rain**. Forests also keep the area cooler and moderate the climate.

steps.title: Soil and water
steps.body:
- Tree roots **bind soil** and prevent **soil erosion**.
- The forest floor and humus act like a **sponge**, soaking rainwater, which seeps into the ground and recharges groundwater.
- This reduces **floods** and keeps rivers flowing steadily.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why are floods more common in areas where forests have been cut?

A: Without trees and humus, rainwater runs off quickly instead of soaking in, and carries soil with it.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How do forests help in rain? → Transpiration adds water vapour to the air, which helps cloud formation and rainfall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking forests only provide wood — they also provide air balance, water, soil protection and homes for wildlife.
- Believing rain depends only on oceans — local forests contribute water vapour too.

statements.s: Forests are called green lungs.
Tree roots increase soil erosion.
Forests help recharge groundwater.
Transpiration from trees can help bring rain.
Cutting forests reduces floods.

quiz.q: Forests are called green lungs because they
quiz.why: Forests take in CO₂ and release oxygen in photosynthesis, which helps balance these gases in the air. So they are called green lungs.
Roots bind the soil and hold it in place. So they prevent soil erosion by wind and water.
The forest floor, with its humus and leaf litter, soaks up rain like a sponge and releases it slowly.

quiz.q: Water vapour from leaves is released by
quiz.why: Plants lose water vapour from their leaves by transpiration. In a forest this adds a lot of moisture to the air.
Without trees, rain washes the soil away and floods become more likely. Deforestation therefore leads to more floods and soil erosion.

scenes.text: Tibu lives in a village near a forest. His family collects honey, tendu leaves, fruits and medicinal herbs.
A plan to clear part of the forest for a factory worries the village.
The villagers meet the officials: they want to protect the forest that protects them.

steps.title: What forests give
steps.body:
- Wood (timber, firewood), bamboo, paper
- **Gum, resin, honey, lac, sealing wax**, catechu, katha
- **Medicinal plants**, spices, fruits, fodder
- Homes (habitat) for wild animals; livelihood for forest dwellers and many communities

steps.title: Dangers
steps.body: **Deforestation** (cutting forests for farms, buildings, roads, industries) causes loss of wildlife, soil erosion, floods, less rain locally, higher CO₂ in the air and harm to forest-dwelling people.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body:
- Plant trees and protect young saplings
- Use paper wisely, recycle, reduce wood use
- Protected areas: national parks and wildlife sanctuaries
- Respect the rights and knowledge of forest communities, who often protect forests best
- Prevent forest fires

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Give two reasons why forest-dwelling communities depend on forests.

A: (1) Food, fuel and medicines; (2) livelihood from honey, leaves, bamboo and other forest products.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How does saving paper help forests? → Less paper means fewer trees cut for wood pulp.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking planting trees anywhere fully replaces an old forest — natural forests have complex layers and species that take decades to develop.
- Forgetting the human side: forest communities are part of the forest.

activity.prompt: My forest-friendly actions this month:
items: Use both sides of notebook pages
Learn the names of 5 trees in my area
Tell my family why forests matter

quiz.why: Honey is a forest product. Glass, plastic and steel are made in factories.
Deforestation means cutting down or clearing forests on a large scale.
Wildlife sanctuaries and national parks are protected areas where wild animals and plants are kept safe.
Paper is made from wood pulp. Saving paper means fewer trees need to be cut.

quiz.q: Forest dwellers depend on forests for
quiz.why: People living in forests get food, fuel, medicines and a livelihood from them. Forests also give them shelter.

questions.q: Roof of tall tree branches in a forest
questions.why: The roof formed by the branches of tall trees is the canopy.

questions.q: Dark fertile substance from decomposed matter
questions.why: Humus is the dark, fertile substance made when dead plants and animals decompose.

questions.q: A food chain starts with
questions.why: A food chain starts with plants, the producers, which make food. Animals and decomposers come later.

questions.q: Forests are called
questions.why: Forests are called green lungs because they take in CO₂ and give out oxygen, helping balance these gases.

questions.q: Decomposers include
questions.why: Bacteria and fungi break down dead matter, and they are the decomposers. Grass is a producer, and deer and lions are consumers.

questions.q: Tree roots help prevent
questions.why: Tree roots hold the soil together, so rain and wind cannot easily wash it away. They prevent soil erosion.

questions.q: Which is NOT a forest product?
questions.why: Lac, honey and gum are collected from forests. Plastic is made in factories from chemicals, so it is not a forest product.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Forests reduce floods. Reason (R): Humus and forest floor soak up rainwater.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: forests reduce floods. R is true: humus and the forest floor soak up rainwater like a sponge, so less runs off. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A food chain can start with a tiger. Reason (R): Tigers are carnivores.
questions.why: A is false: a food chain starts with a producer, which is a plant. R is true that tigers are carnivores, but that is why they come at the end.

questions.q: Correct food chain
questions.why: In a food chain, energy goes from producer to herbivore to carnivore. So grass is eaten by deer, and deer by tiger. The arrows point to the eater.

questions.q: Forest helps in rainfall mainly by
questions.why: Trees release water vapour by transpiration, which adds moisture to the air and helps form clouds and rain.

questions.q: Case: A hill slope was cleared of trees. Next monsoon, the stream below became muddy. Reason?
options: Soil washed down due to no roots binding it
questions.why: With the trees gone, no roots bind the soil. Monsoon rain washes it down the slope into the stream, making it muddy.

questions.q: Case: If all the deer in a forest were hunted, what would happen to tigers and grass?
questions.why: Tigers eat deer, so they would lose food and decline. With fewer deer to eat it, the grass may grow too much.

questions.q: Why are decomposers called the cleaning agents of the forest?
options: They break down dead matter and recycle nutrients
questions.why: Decomposers break down dead plants and animals and return nutrients to the soil. This clears the forest of dead matter and recycles nutrients.

questions.q: Increasing deforestation leads to more CO₂ in the air because
options: fewer trees absorb CO₂ in photosynthesis
questions.why: Trees take in CO₂ for photosynthesis. With fewer trees, less CO₂ is removed from the air, so more stays in it.

questions.q: Which layer of a forest would shade-loving herbs prefer?
questions.why: Shade-loving herbs need little light. The forest floor and lower layers get the least sunlight, so they grow there.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Wastewater Story
courses.summary: What sewage contains, how the sewerage network carries it, step-by-step treatment in a wastewater treatment plant, what we should never pour down the drain, and sanitation solutions where there are no sewers.
outcomes: Learners can describe what sewage is and what it contains
Learners can explain each stage of a wastewater treatment plant
Learners can practise good housekeeping to reduce pollution of wastewater
Learners can describe sanitation options and their link to health

story.title: Where does the bath water go?

scenes.text: After her bath, Paheli watches the water swirl down the drain.
"Where does it go? Does it come back to our tap?"
Her teacher shows a map of underground pipes leading to a treatment plant outside the city.

steps.title: Our lifeline
steps.body: Clean water is essential, yet many people lack access to safe water. **World Water Day** is observed on **22 March** each year to draw attention to this. Cleaning water before it re-enters water bodies is called **sewage treatment** or wastewater treatment.

steps.title: What sewage is
steps.body:
**Sewage** is wastewater released by homes, industries, hospitals, offices and other users; it also includes rainwater that runs down streets carrying harmful substances. It is a complex mixture:

- **Organic impurities**: human faeces, animal waste, oil, urea (urine), pesticides, herbicides, fruit and vegetable waste
- **Inorganic impurities**: nitrates, phosphates, metals
- **Nutrients**: phosphorus, nitrogen
- **Bacteria**: e.g. those causing cholera and typhoid
- **Other microbes**: e.g. those causing dysentery

steps.title: Sewerage
steps.body: A network of big and small pipes called **sewers** forming the **sewerage** carries sewage from where it is produced to the point of disposal (treatment plant). **Manholes** are placed at intervals (about 50–60 m) and at junctions so workers can access the sewers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Name two organic and two inorganic impurities in sewage.

A: Organic: human faeces, food waste. Inorganic: nitrates, phosphates (or metals).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: What is the difference between sewage and sewerage?

A: Sewage is the wastewater itself; sewerage is the network of pipes that carries it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking wastewater is 'just dirty water' — it carries disease-causing microbes and chemicals.
- Mixing up sewage (liquid) and sewer (pipe).

activity.prompt: Classify the impurity in sewage.

quiz.why: World Water Day is observed every year on 22 March. It reminds us to save and protect water.
Sewage is the dirty wastewater from homes, industries, hospitals and other places. It needs treatment before it is released.
Sewerage is the network of pipes that carries sewage. Sewage is the waste itself, and sludge is the solid settled part.
Nitrates are inorganic impurities in sewage. Faeces, food waste and urea come from living things, so they are organic.

options: access sewers for cleaning and repair
quiz.why: Manholes let workers go down to inspect, clean and repair the sewer pipes.

story.title: A visit to the treatment plant

scenes.text: The class visits a wastewater treatment plant (WWTP).
First, big screens catch rags, sticks, plastic bags and cans.
At the end of a long journey, the water leaving the plant is clear enough to be released into a river.

steps.title: Physical stages
steps.body:
1. **Bar screens**: remove large objects — rags, sticks, cans, plastic packets, napkins.
2. **Grit and sand removal tank**: wastewater flows slowly so sand, grit and pebbles settle.
3. **Primary clarifier (large settling tank)**: solids like faeces settle at the bottom as **sludge**, scraped out by a scraper; a **skimmer** removes floating **oil and grease**. The water left is **clarified water**.

steps.title: Biological stage
steps.body:
4. **Aeration tank**: air is pumped into the clarified water to help **aerobic bacteria** grow. They consume human waste, food waste, soaps and other unwanted matter.
5. After several hours, the microbes settle as **activated sludge** (about 97% water). Water is removed by sand drying beds or machines; the dried sludge is used as **manure**.
6. Treated water has very low levels of organic material and suspended matter. It is discharged into a sea, river or ground. Sometimes it is **disinfected with chlorine and ozone** first.

steps.title: Sludge and biogas
steps.body: Sludge from the settling tank is transferred to a separate tank where **anaerobic bacteria** decompose it, producing **biogas**, which can be used as fuel or to produce electricity.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Arrange: aeration tank, bar screen, primary clarifier, grit chamber. → **Bar screen → grit and sand removal → primary clarifier → aeration tank**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why is air bubbled through the clarified water?

A: To support aerobic bacteria that consume the remaining organic waste.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking treatment makes water fit to drink directly — it is made safe to release; drinking water needs further purification.
- Mixing aerobic bacteria (aeration tank) with anaerobic bacteria (biogas from sludge).

activity.prompt: Order the stages of wastewater treatment.
items: Primary clarifier: sludge settles, skimmer removes oil
Aeration tank: aerobic bacteria digest waste
Activated sludge settles and is removed

quiz.why: Bar screens are the first step in treatment. They remove large objects such as rags, sticks and plastic.

quiz.q: Floating oil and grease are removed by a
quiz.why: A skimmer removes floating oil and grease from the top of the water. A bar screen takes out large objects.
Air is pumped into the water so that aerobic bacteria, which need oxygen, can grow and break down the waste.
Activated sludge is mostly water, about 97%. The rest is solid matter that settles out.

quiz.q: Biogas is produced from sludge by
quiz.why: Anaerobic bacteria break down sludge without oxygen. This gives biogas, which can be used as fuel.

quiz.q: Treated water may be disinfected with
quiz.why: After treatment the water can be disinfected with chlorine or ozone, which kill the germs that remain.

lessons.title: Better housekeeping: what not to pour down the drain

scenes.text: Every day, Mother poured leftover frying oil into the kitchen sink.
One morning the drain was completely blocked!
The plumber explained: oil hardens in pipes. Wipe it with paper and throw it in the dustbin.

steps.title: Keep out of drains
steps.body:
- **Cooking oil and fats**: harden and block pipes; in open drains they clog soil pores and reduce filtering.
- **Chemicals** (paints, solvents, insecticides, motor oil, medicines): kill the useful microbes that purify water.
- **Solid wastes**: tea leaves, food remains, cotton, soft toys, sanitary towels — block drains and stop oxygen flowing, hampering treatment.

Throw them in the dustbin or give them for proper disposal.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Less pollution at the source means easier, cheaper treatment and cleaner rivers. **Reduce, reuse, recycle**: use wastewater from washing vegetables to water plants.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why should medicines not be flushed?

A: They kill helpful microbes in treatment plants and can pollute rivers.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How can a family reduce wastewater pollution? → Wipe greasy pans before washing, put food scraps in a compost bin, store old paint for safe disposal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking hot water carries oil safely away — it cools and sticks further down the pipe.
- Flushing wet wipes or cotton because they 'disappear' — they block sewers.

activity.prompt: Where should it go?

quiz.why: Cooking oil and fat cool and harden inside the pipes. They stick and build up, blocking the drains.
Chemicals like paint kill the useful microbes that clean the water. This makes treatment harder.
Tea leaves are solid waste and would block pipes. They belong in the dustbin or compost, not the sink or toilet.

quiz.q: Water used for washing vegetables can be
quiz.why: Water used to wash vegetables is fairly clean. It can be reused to water plants, which saves water.
Wet wipes do not break down easily and clog sewers. They should go in the dustbin.

scenes.text: Ramnagar village has no sewer pipes. People used to defecate in the open.
Every monsoon, cholera and diarrhoea spread from contaminated water.
With toilets connected to septic tanks and composting pits, illness fell sharply.

steps.title: Open defecation and health
steps.body: Untreated human excreta pollutes soil and water, including groundwater. It is a major cause of diseases like **cholera, typhoid, polio, meningitis, hepatitis and dysentery**. Proper sanitation is essential for public health.

steps.title: Low-cost onsite sanitation
steps.body:
Where there is no sewerage:

- **Septic tanks**: for places without sewers (hospitals, isolated buildings, small groups of houses).
- **Chemical toilets**: e.g. in trains, buses and events.
- **Composting pits**.
- **Vermi-processing toilets**: human excreta is treated by **earthworms**, producing high-quality manure (vermi cakes); the design has been tried in India.
- Some plants link toilets to **biogas plants**, producing energy from excreta.

steps.title: Sanitation in public places
steps.body: Fairs, railway stations, bus depots, airports and hospitals produce large amounts of waste. Proper disposal and clean toilets are essential to prevent epidemics. **We must not litter, spit or urinate in public places.** Planting **eucalyptus trees** along sewage ponds is suggested because they absorb surplus wastewater rapidly and release pure water vapour into the air.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How do vermi-processing toilets work? → Earthworms feed on and break down human waste, turning it into manure.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why should a railway station keep toilets clean and drains covered?

A: Thousands of people pass daily; dirty toilets and open waste spread disease quickly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking open defecation affects only the person — it pollutes water for the whole community.
- Believing sanitation is only the government's job; each of us must use toilets, keep surroundings clean and wash hands with soap.

activity.prompt: My sanitation habits:
items: I always use a toilet and flush/clean it
I wash my hands with soap after using the toilet and before eating
I never throw solid waste into drains
I do not litter or spit in public places
I report open drains or overflowing sewers to adults/authorities

quiz.q: Diseases spread by poor sanitation include
quiz.why: Poor sanitation lets germs reach drinking water, causing water-borne diseases like cholera and typhoid. Myopia, sunburn and fractures are not caused by it.

quiz.q: Toilets in which earthworms treat excreta
quiz.why: Vermi-processing toilets use earthworms to break down excreta. They are a low-cost way to treat waste on site.
Eucalyptus trees take up a lot of water, so planting them near sewage ponds helps absorb the extra water.
Septic tanks treat waste on site, so they are useful where there is no sewer network.
Untreated excreta can seep into the soil and pollute groundwater, which people may then drink or use, spreading disease.

questions.q: Wastewater from homes and industries is called
questions.why: Wastewater from homes and industries is called sewage. Sewerage is the pipe system, and sludge is the settled solid part.

questions.q: First step in a WWTP
questions.why: Bar screens come first in a treatment plant. They take out large objects before the later steps.

questions.q: World Water Day
questions.why: World Water Day is on 22 March each year.

questions.q: Gas produced from sludge
questions.why: When anaerobic bacteria break down sludge, they give out biogas. It can be used as fuel.

questions.q: Skimmer removes
questions.why: A skimmer takes off oil and grease that float on top of the water. Heavier solids settle instead.

questions.q: Aerobic bacteria are encouraged in the
questions.why: The aeration tank has air pumped in, so aerobic bacteria can grow there. They digest the waste.

questions.q: Dried sludge is used as
questions.why: Dried sludge is rich in nutrients and can be used as manure for plants. The biogas from it can be used as fuel.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Cooking oil should not be poured into drains. Reason (R): It hardens and blocks pipes.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: oil should not go in the drain. R is true: it hardens and blocks the pipes. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Treated wastewater can be safely drunk directly. Reason (R): Treated water has low organic matter.
questions.why: A is false: treated wastewater is fit to release into water bodies but not to drink without more treatment. R is true that it has less organic matter, but that does not make it safe to drink.

questions.q: Which disinfectants may be used on treated water?
questions.why: Treated water can be disinfected with chlorine or ozone to kill germs. Oil, grease, nitrates, sand and grit are impurities.

questions.q: Which is NOT an impurity in sewage?
questions.why: Urea, pesticides and nitrates are impurities in sewage. Oxygen in pure air is a normal part of air and is not an impurity.

questions.q: Case: Sanitary napkins and cotton are flushed in a housing society. Effect on the sewer?
questions.why: Such solid waste does not break down. It collects in the pipes, blocking the sewer and causing overflow.

questions.q: Case: A town has no sewerage. Best low-cost option for a hospital there?
questions.why: Without a sewer network, a septic tank treats waste on site at low cost. Dumping or open drains would spread disease.

questions.q: Why are microbes in a treatment plant harmed by chemicals in sewage?
options: Chemicals like paints and solvents kill them
questions.why: Chemicals such as paints and solvents kill the useful microbes that clean the water. So they should not be put into drains.

questions.q: In which order is sludge handled?
options: settles in clarifier → anaerobic digestion → biogas and manure
questions.why: Sludge settles in the clarifier. It is then broken down by anaerobic bacteria in a digester, giving biogas and manure. The other orders do not match the process.

questions.q: Why are manholes provided at regular intervals in sewers?
options: To add oxygen to drinking water
For workers to inspect and clean the sewer
questions.why: Manholes let workers get into the sewer to inspect and clean it regularly. They are not for decoration.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Class 7 Science
courses.summary: A complete revision of Class 7 Science — key terms, word equations, processes and diagrams described in words — followed by two mock papers mixing MCQ, assertion–reason and case-based questions.
outcomes: Learners can recall key definitions and word equations from every chapter
Learners can explain processes such as photosynthesis, digestion, respiration and wastewater treatment
Learners can solve speed and temperature numericals
Learners can attempt assertion–reason and case-based questions confidently

scenes.text: Tanvi has her science exam tomorrow.
She revises biology chapters in one sheet: plants, animals, respiration, transport, reproduction, forests.
For each line, she says it aloud and gives an example.

steps.title: Nutrition
steps.body:
- Autotrophs make food; heterotrophs take ready-made food
- Carbon dioxide + water → (sunlight, chlorophyll) → carbohydrate + oxygen
- Iodine + starch → blue-black
- Cuscuta: parasite; pitcher plant: insectivorous; fungi: saprotrophs; lichen and Rhizobium–legume: symbiosis
- Ingestion → digestion → absorption → assimilation → egestion
- Teeth: incisors 8, canines 4, premolars 8, molars 12
- Liver → bile (stored in gall bladder) → fats; villi absorb; ruminants chew cud; Amoeba uses pseudopodia and food vacuole

steps.title: Respiration and transport
steps.body:
- Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → CO₂ + water + energy
- Anaerobic (yeast): glucose → alcohol + CO₂ + energy; (muscle): glucose → lactic acid + energy
- Inhale: ribs up/out, diaphragm down; exhale: ribs down/in, diaphragm up
- Cockroach: spiracles & tracheae; earthworm: skin; fish: gills
- Blood: plasma, RBC (haemoglobin), WBC, platelets; arteries from heart, veins to heart; pulse 72–80/min
- Heart: 4 chambers; kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra
- Xylem: water & minerals; phloem: food; transpiration

steps.title: Reproduction and forests
steps.body:
- Asexual: vegetative propagation, budding (yeast), fragmentation (Spirogyra), spores (mould, fern)
- Stamen (anther, filament) and pistil (stigma, style, ovary); pollination → fertilisation → zygote → embryo
- Ovary → fruit, ovule → seed; dispersal by wind, water, animals, explosion
- Forest layers: canopy, understorey, herbs; decomposers make humus; forests = green lungs

steps.title: Model answer
steps.body:
Q: Why do we feel tired and get cramps after a long run? Explain with word equation.

A: Muscles respire anaerobically when oxygen is short: glucose → lactic acid + energy. Lactic acid builds up and causes cramps; massage or a hot bath improves blood flow and oxygen supply.

steps.title: Frequent slips
steps.body:
- Bile is made in the liver, not the gall bladder.
- Pulmonary artery carries CO₂-rich blood.
- Plants respire day and night.

quiz.why: Phloem carries food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant. Xylem carries water and minerals.
A lichen is an alga and a fungus living together, and both benefit. This partnership is symbiosis.
An earthworm breathes through its moist skin. It has no lungs, gills or tracheae.
After fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed. The ovary becomes the fruit.
Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter in the forest and form humus.

lessons.title: Revision sheet: physical and material world

scenes.text: Tanvi's brother is weak in numericals and word equations.
They make one sheet with every formula and reaction from Class 7.
He solves 10 practice sums and gets them all right.

steps.title: Heat and acids
steps.body:
- Clinical thermometer 35–42 °C; lab thermometer −10–110 °C; normal body temperature about 37 °C
- Conduction (solids), convection (fluids; sea breeze by day, land breeze by night), radiation (no medium)
- Acid turns blue litmus red; base turns red litmus blue; turmeric → red in base; china rose → magenta (acid), green (base)
- Acid + base → salt + water + heat

steps.title: Changes
steps.body:
- Magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide; magnesium oxide + water → magnesium hydroxide
- Copper sulphate + iron → iron sulphate + copper
- Vinegar + baking soda → CO₂ + other substances; CO₂ + lime water → calcium carbonate + water
- Iron + oxygen + water → rust; prevent by paint, grease, galvanising (zinc)
- Crystallisation is a physical change

steps.title: Motion, electricity, light, wastewater
steps.body:
- Speed = distance ÷ time; 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s; time period = total time ÷ number of oscillations
- Fuse/MCB protect; heating effect: heater, iron; magnetic effect: Oersted, electromagnet, electric bell
- Plane mirror: erect, same size, virtual, laterally inverted; concave: torches, dentists; convex: rear-view mirrors
- Convex lens: converging, magnifier; concave lens: diverging; VIBGYOR
- WWTP: bar screen → grit removal → clarifier → aeration → activated sludge → disinfection

steps.title: Model numerical
steps.body:
A car's odometer goes from 4520 km to 4610 km between 9:00 and 10:30. Find its average speed in km/h and m/s.

- Distance = 90 km; time = 1.5 h
- Speed = 60 km/h = 60 × 5/18 ≈ **16.7 m/s**

steps.title: Frequent slips
steps.body:
- Land breeze is at night, sea breeze by day.
- Electromagnets lose magnetism when current stops.
- Convex mirrors never form real images.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its fact.

quiz.why: Rusting forms a new substance, iron oxide, so it is chemical. Crystallisation, dissolving and melting give no new substance.
Multiply km/h by 5/18 to get m/s. 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.
Turmeric turns red with bases, such as soap solution. It stays yellow in acids.

quiz.q: Heat from the Sun reaches us by
quiz.why: Heat reaches us from the Sun across empty space, with no medium. That is radiation, not conduction or convection.

quiz.q: Aerobic bacteria are used in the
quiz.why: The aeration tank has air pumped in, which helps aerobic bacteria break down waste.

scenes.text: Arjun used to write one line for 3-mark questions and lose marks.
His teacher shows him: definition + explanation + example/diagram-in-words.
Now his answers earn full marks.

steps.title: Structure of good answers
steps.body:
- 1 mark: one clear fact or term
- 2 marks: fact + reason, or two points
- 3 marks: definition + explanation + example (or word equation)
- 5 marks: introduce, explain each step in order, give example/labelled description, conclude

steps.title: Experiment questions
steps.body: Learn for each activity: **aim, materials, method, observation, conclusion, precautions**. Common ones: starch test, litmus tests, lime water test for CO₂, rusting test tubes, crystallisation, pendulum time period, electromagnet, transpiration bag.

steps.title: Model 3-mark answer
steps.body:
Q: What is transpiration? Give two uses.

A: Loss of water as vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through stomata. (1) It creates a suction pull that helps lift water up tall plants. (2) It cools the plant.

steps.title: Model experiment answer
steps.body: Aim: to show CO₂ is produced when vinegar reacts with baking soda. Method: add vinegar to baking soda in a test tube fitted with a bent tube dipping into lime water. Observation: fizzing; lime water turns milky. Conclusion: CO₂ is produced. Precaution: use small amounts; hold the tube away from your face.

steps.title: Common answer mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing a long story without the key term.
- Missing units in numericals.
- Skipping precautions in experiment answers.

activity.prompt: Exam-day checklist:
items: Practise 3 speed numericals with unit conversions
Recall aims and observations of 8 activities
Sleep well and carry pens, pencil, eraser, scale

quiz.why: A 3-mark answer should give a definition, an explanation and an example, so that each point can earn a mark.
Lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide, forming calcium carbonate. This is the test for CO₂.
Timing several oscillations and dividing gives a more accurate time period, because a small timing error is shared out.

quiz.q: Observation in the starch test of a sunlit leaf
quiz.why: A leaf kept in sunlight makes starch, which gives a blue-black colour with iodine.
Numericals should always have units with the answer. A number without its unit is incomplete.

questions.q: Iodine test detects
questions.why: Iodine solution turns blue-black when starch is present. It does not show vitamins, proteins or fats.

questions.q: Organ that stores bile
questions.why: The liver makes bile, and the gall bladder stores it until it is needed to digest fat.

questions.q: Unit of speed
questions.why: Speed is distance per time, so its SI unit is metre per second (m/s). Kilogram, second and metre are units of mass, time and length.

questions.q: Acid in ant sting
questions.why: An ant sting contains formic acid. A mild base such as calamine eases it.

questions.q: Convection occurs in
questions.why: Convection needs particles that can flow, so it happens in fluids, that is, liquids and gases. It cannot happen in solids or in vacuum.

questions.q: Spores are formed by
questions.why: Bread mould is a fungus and reproduces by spores. Potato and rose are grown from vegetative parts, and yeast reproduces by budding.

questions.q: An electric bell works on
questions.why: An electric bell works on the magnetic effect of current. An electromagnet pulls the strip so the hammer strikes the gong.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Reason (R): They have thin walls with valves.
questions.why: A is true: arteries carry blood away from the heart. R is false: arteries have thick, elastic walls, and it is veins that have valves.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Pitcher plants are partly heterotrophic. Reason (R): They obtain nitrogen from trapped insects.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: pitcher plants make food but also trap insects, so they are partly heterotrophic. R is true: they get nitrogen from the insects, which is the reason they trap them.

questions.q: Pendulum: 25 oscillations in 50 s. Time period
questions.why: Time period = total time ÷ oscillations = 50 ÷ 25 = 2 s.

questions.q: CO₂ through lime water forms
questions.why: CO₂ reacts with lime water (calcium hydroxide) to form calcium carbonate. This makes the water milky.

questions.q: Case: A fish tank's air pump fails overnight; fish come to the surface gasping. Why?
questions.why: Fish breathe oxygen that is dissolved in the water. If the pump stops, the dissolved oxygen falls, so fish come up to gasp at the surface.

questions.q: Case: A cyclist covers 6 km in 20 minutes, then 4 km in 20 minutes. Average speed in km/h?
questions.why: Total distance = 6 + 4 = 10 km. Total time = 20 + 20 = 40 min = 2/3 h. Average speed = 10 ÷ (2/3) = 15 km/h.

questions.q: Case: A farmer finds blue litmus turns red with his soil solution. What should he add?
questions.why: Blue litmus turning red shows the soil is acidic. A base like lime (calcium hydroxide) will neutralise it. Vinegar is an acid.

questions.q: Case: In a WWTP, the aeration blower stops for a day. Which process slows most?
options: digestion of waste by aerobic bacteria
questions.why: Aerobic bacteria that digest the waste need the air supplied by the blower. Without air, that digestion slows most. Screens, grit settling and skimming do not use air.

questions.q: A student says: "A convex lens and a convex mirror both form real images of distant objects." Correct?
questions.why: A convex lens can form real images of distant objects. A convex mirror always forms virtual, smaller images, so the student is only partly right.

questions.q: Which is correctly matched?
questions.why: Rhizobium lives in root nodules of legumes. Ferns reproduce by spores, yeast by budding, and Cuscuta is a parasite, not a symbiont.

questions.q: Ritu stands 4 m from a plane mirror. She moves 1 m away from it. New distance between Ritu and her image?
questions.why: After she moves 1 m away, she is 4 + 1 = 5 m from the mirror. Her image is also 5 m behind it, so the distance is 5 + 5 = 10 m.

school-c7-social-a.title: Class 7 Social Science · Part A
school-c7-social-a.description: Class 7 History (Our Pasts–II), Geography (Our Environment) and Civics (Social and Political Life–II), chapter by chapter, with timelines, case studies and chapter tests.

courses.title: Ch 1 · Tracing Changes Through a Thousand Years (History)
courses.summary: How historians study the period from about 700 to 1750 CE: changing maps and words, manuscripts and chronicles, new technologies, foods and social groups, regions and empires, and how history is divided into periods.
outcomes: Learners can explain why old maps and terms must be read in their context
Learners can describe sources historians use for this period and their problems
Learners can list new technologies, crops and social groups of the period
Learners can critique the old Hindu–Muslim–British division of Indian history

lessons.title: Maps and changing meanings of words

scenes.text: The teacher shows a map of the subcontinent drawn by the Arab geographer al-Idrisi in 1154. South India is at the top!
A French map from 1720 looks far more like the maps we use today.
Maps, like words, change their meaning over time. Historians must read them in context.

steps.title: Maps through time
steps.body:
- **Al-Idrisi's map (1154 CE)**: part of a larger world map; north and south are reversed compared with modern maps, and place names are in Arabic.
- **A French cartographer's map (1720 CE)**: closer to modern maps because mapmaking had become more scientific.

The **science of mapmaking (cartography)** changed over the centuries, so old maps must be understood in their own setting.

steps.title: Words that changed meaning
steps.body:
- **Hindustan**: in the 13th century the Persian chronicler **Minhaj-i Siraj** used it for the lands of Punjab, Haryana and the region between the Ganga and Yamuna — the areas under the Delhi Sultan. In the early 16th century **Babur** used it for the geography, animals and culture of the subcontinent. It did not mean the modern nation 'India'.
- **Foreigner**: in medieval times it meant any stranger not part of a particular society or culture — a city dweller might call a forest dweller a foreigner. Two peasants in the same village were not foreigners to each other even if they followed different religions.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why is al-Idrisi's map 'upside down' to us?

A: Mapmaking conventions differed; he placed south at the top. It is not an error — just a different way of drawing.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Did 'Hindustan' in Minhaj-i Siraj's writing include Tamil Nadu?

A: No. It meant only Punjab, Haryana and the Ganga–Yamuna lands under the Sultanate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading old words with today's meanings.
- Thinking old maps were 'wrong' — they followed different rules.

activity.prompt: Match the term or source with its meaning.
pairs: A stranger to a particular society
Geography, fauna and culture of the subcontinent

quiz.why: Al-Idrisi, an Arab geographer, drew his world map in 1154 CE, in the 12th century.
Minhaj-i Siraj was a chronicler of the Delhi Sultans who wrote in Persian, the language of the court.
In medieval times a foreigner meant any stranger, someone not part of that society. It could even be a person from another village or town.
A cartographer is a person who makes maps.

options: the geography, fauna and culture of the subcontinent
quiz.why: Babur used the word Hindustan for the geography, animals and culture of the subcontinent. It was not a nation-state as now.

scenes.text: In the 14th century, the chronicler Ziyauddin Barani wrote his history in 1356.
Two years later he wrote another version — and the two differ!
Historians compare versions and copies carefully before trusting any detail.

steps.title: More sources than before
steps.body: For 700–1750 CE, historians use **coins, inscriptions, architecture and textual records**. Textual records increased greatly because **paper** became cheaper and widely available. People wrote holy texts, chronicles of rulers, letters, teachings of saints, petitions, judicial records, accounts and taxes.

steps.title: Manuscripts and scribes
steps.body: There was no printing press. **Manuscripts** were written and copied by hand by **scribes**. While copying, scribes made small changes — a word here, a sentence there. Over centuries copies became different from the original. Since the original (author's) manuscript is rarely available, historians compare many copies to guess what was first written. Authors also revised their own works, as Barani did in 1356 and 1358.

steps.title: Archives
steps.body: Libraries and **archives** (places where documents and manuscripts are stored) were kept by kings, monasteries and temples.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why are scribes' copies a problem for historians?

A: Small changes made while copying add up over time, so copies differ; historians must compare them to find the most likely original wording.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why did written records increase in this period? → Paper became cheaper and more available.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming every manuscript copy says exactly what the author wrote.
- Forgetting non-written sources like coins and buildings.

activity.prompt: Is it a written (textual) source or a material source?

quiz.why: Before printing, books and records were written by hand. Such handwritten documents are manuscripts.
Scribes were the people who copied manuscripts by hand.

quiz.q: A place where documents are stored
quiz.why: An archive is a place where documents and records are stored and kept safe.

quiz.q: Barani wrote his chronicle first in
quiz.why: Barani wrote his chronicle, the Fatawa-i Jahandari, first in about 1356 and revised it a couple of years later.
Paper became cheaper and more available, so more people could write and copy documents.

lessons.title: New social and political groups; regions and empires

story.title: A plate of chillies and potatoes

scenes.text: Grandma's aloo-mirch is a favourite at home.
But potatoes, corn and chillies came to India from the Americas only in this period!
New foods, tools and people transformed the subcontinent over a thousand years.

steps.title: New technologies and crops
steps.body:
- **Persian wheel** in irrigation, **spinning wheel** in weaving, **firearms** in combat
- New foods and beverages: **potatoes, corn, chillies, tea and coffee** (many from the Americas)
- Movement of people brought new ideas, as did trade.

steps.title: New groups
steps.body: Groups that became important: **Rajputs** (from 'rajaputra', son of a ruler) — warriors who admired chivalry and loyalty; **Marathas, Sikhs, Jats, Ahoms and Kayasthas** (scribes and secretaries). Many forest dwellers cleared land and became peasants. Society was organised into **jatis** (sub-castes), regulated by their own rules and assemblies (**jati panchayats**).

steps.title: Region and empire
steps.body: Large states covered many regions. The **Delhi Sultanate** and later the **Mughals** built empires; a Sanskrit prashasti of 1276 even praised the Delhi Sultan **Ghiyasuddin Balban** as ruler of a vast region. Yet regions kept their own languages, customs and identities; when empires declined in the 18th century, regional states re-emerged.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Name two technologies that spread in this period and their use. → Persian wheel (irrigation), spinning wheel (weaving).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: What did jati panchayats do?

A: They framed rules and regulations for members of a jati, settled disputes and enforced the rules.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking chillies and potatoes are ancient Indian crops — they came from the Americas.
- Assuming 'Rajput' was one family — it was a broad group of warrior families.

statements.s: Chillies came to India from the Americas.
statements.why: Part of the exchange after European voyages.

statements.s: The Persian wheel was used for irrigation.
Kayasthas were mainly warriors.
Jatis had their own rules and assemblies.
Regional identities disappeared under empires.

quiz.q: Which crop came from the Americas?
quiz.why: Potato came from the Americas, so it was a new crop in the subcontinent. Rice, barley and wheat were already grown.
Rajput comes from rajaputra, meaning son of a ruler.
Kayasthas were a caste of scribes and secretaries who kept records.
Jati panchayats were assemblies of a jati that made rules and settled disputes for its members.
A Sanskrit inscription of 1276 CE praised the Delhi Sultan Ghiyasuddin Balban.

scenes.text: A 19th-century British historian, James Mill, divided Indian history into "Hindu", "Muslim" and "British" periods.
Modern historians disagree: it ignores the rich variety within each period.
Today we often use "ancient", "medieval" and "modern" — and even these have limits.

steps.title: Changes in religion
steps.body: Important developments: worship of new deities, temple building by royalty, growing importance of **Brahmanas**; the idea of **bhakti** (a loving, personal deity reached through devotion). Merchants and migrants brought **Islam**; rulers patronised it and the **ulama** (learned theologians and jurists). Muslims were divided into **Shia** (who believed the Prophet's son-in-law Ali was the rightful leader) and **Sunni** (who accepted the authority of the early Khalifas); there were also different schools of law, such as Hanafi and Shafi'i.

steps.title: Periodisation
steps.body: **James Mill** (a Scottish economist and political philosopher) divided Indian history into Hindu, Muslim and British periods, and thought all Asian societies less advanced than Europe. This view ignored diversity and was based on prejudice. Historians now look at economic and social factors and use 'ancient', 'medieval' and 'modern' — though the 'modern' label wrongly suggests that only change brought from the West counts as progress.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why do historians reject Mill's periodisation?

A: It labels whole periods by the religion of rulers, ignores the variety of people and practices, and assumes Asia was backward.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Who were the ulama? → Learned scholars of Islam who interpreted Islamic law and theology.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all people in a 'Muslim period' were Muslim or all in a 'Hindu period' were Hindu.
- Treating period labels as exact walls; changes were gradual.

activity.prompt: Arrange these in time order.

events.text: Barani writes the first version of his chronicle
A French cartographer's map of the subcontinent

quiz.q: James Mill divided Indian history into
quiz.why: James Mill divided Indian history into Hindu, Muslim and British periods, based on the religion of the rulers. Historians now find this unsuitable.
The ulama were learned Islamic scholars, such as theologians and jurists.

options: loving devotion to a personal deity
quiz.why: Bhakti is loving devotion to a personal god or goddess.
Historians today look beyond rulers and wars to economic and social changes in people's lives.

quiz.q: Shias believed the rightful leader after the Prophet was
quiz.why: Shias believed that Ali, the Prophet's son-in-law, was the rightful leader of the Muslim community after him.

questions.q: Period covered by Our Pasts–II
questions.why: The textbook Our Pasts–II covers about a thousand years, from roughly 700 to 1750 CE.

questions.q: Handwritten documents are called
questions.why: Handwritten documents are called manuscripts. Printing came much later.

questions.q: Al-Idrisi was a
questions.why: Al-Idrisi was an Arab geographer who made a famous map of the world in 1154.

questions.q: Which is a new food of this period?
questions.why: Chilli came from the Americas during this period. Rice, millets and wheat were already grown in the subcontinent.

questions.q: A place for storing documents
questions.why: An archive is a place for storing documents. A mint makes coins.

questions.q: Minhaj-i Siraj used "Hindustan" for
questions.why: In the 13th century Minhaj-i Siraj used Hindustan for Punjab, Haryana and the lands between the Ganga and the Yamuna. The meaning later widened.

questions.q: Rajputs were known for
questions.why: Rajputs were known as warriors, with ideals of bravery, loyalty and chivalry.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Historians compare several copies of a manuscript. Reason (R): Scribes made small changes while copying.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: historians compare several copies to find the original. R is true: scribes made small changes when copying, so copies differ. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Mill's periodisation is widely accepted today. Reason (R): It labels periods by the religion of rulers.
questions.why: A is false: Mill's scheme is not widely accepted today. R is true that it names periods by the rulers' religion, but that is the reason it is criticised.

questions.q: Why did the number of written records increase?
options: Paper became cheaper and more widely available
questions.why: Paper became cheaper and easier to get, so more people could write and copy documents. This increased written records.

questions.q: Medieval "foreigner" could describe
options: a city dweller speaking of a forest dweller
a neighbour of the same village
questions.why: A foreigner then meant any stranger to a society, such as a city dweller speaking of a forest dweller.

questions.q: Case: A scholar finds two versions of a 14th-century chronicle by the same author, two years apart. What is the best explanation?
options: The author revised his own work
questions.why: Barani revised his own chronicle a couple of years after the first version, so two versions exist. This is a normal reason for different versions.

questions.q: Case: A student says "Hindustan in Babur's writings means the Republic of India." Best correction?
options: Babur used it for the subcontinent's geography, fauna and culture, not a modern nation-state
questions.why: Hindustan in Babur's time was a region with its own geography, fauna and culture. It did not mean the modern nation-state.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: The Persian wheel was used to lift water for irrigation. The other pairs are mismatched.

questions.q: Why is the label "modern" also problematic?
options: It suggests only Western-introduced change is progress
questions.why: Calling a period modern suggests that only change brought by the West is progress. This ignores change in earlier times, so the label is criticised.

questions.q: Which best describes regions in this period?
options: They were all ruled from Paris
They kept their own languages and customs even within empires
questions.why: Regions kept their own languages, customs and identities even when they were part of big empires.

courses.title: Ch 2 · New Kings and Kingdoms (History)
courses.summary: The rise of new dynasties from the 7th century, how kings governed and collected revenue, the struggle for Kanauj, raids for wealth, and the Chola kingdom with its temples, irrigation and village assemblies.
outcomes: Learners can explain how samantas became new rulers and how dynasties were established
Learners can describe administration, revenue and prashastis
Learners can explain the tripartite struggle and the raids of Mahmud of Ghazni
Learners can describe Chola rule, temples, agriculture and local assemblies

scenes.text: In the 8th century, Dantidurga was a Rashtrakuta chief serving the Chalukya kings of Karnataka.
He overthrew his overlord and performed a grand ritual to become a king.
All over the subcontinent, ambitious subordinates were becoming rulers.

steps.title: Samantas
steps.body: By the 7th century there were big landlords and warrior chiefs called **samantas**. Kings recognised them as subordinates; they brought gifts, were present at court and provided military support. As samantas gained power and wealth, many declared themselves **maha-samanta, maha-mandaleshvara** (great lord of a region) and became independent.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Rashtrakutas** (Deccan): **Dantidurga** overthrew his Chalukya overlord in the mid-8th century and performed the **hiranya-garbha** ('golden womb') ritual, believed to cause the rebirth of a person as a Kshatriya even if not one by birth.
- **Kadamba Mayurasharman** and **Gurjara-Pratihara Harichandra** were Brahmanas who gave up their traditional professions and took up arms, establishing kingdoms in Karnataka and Rajasthan.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: What was the hiranya-garbha ritual?

A: A ritual performed with the help of Brahmanas, believed to lead to the 'rebirth' of the sacrificer as a Kshatriya.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How did samantas become independent? → By building up power and wealth, then claiming higher titles and breaking away from their overlords.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking only Kshatriyas by birth could become kings — Brahmanas and others did too.
- Confusing samantas (subordinate chiefs) with sultans.

pairs: Kadamba; Brahmana who took up arms

Dantidurga was a Rashtrakuta ruler in the Deccan.

Many new dynasties arose from about the 7th century CE.

scenes.text: A court poet composes a long Sanskrit poem praising his king as brave, generous and wise.
It is carved on stone in a temple.
Historians read such prashastis carefully — they show how kings wanted to be seen, not always what was true.

steps.title: How kingdoms were run
steps.body: Kings took grand titles (maharaja-adhiraja, tribhuvana-chakravartin). They shared power with samantas and with associations of peasants, traders and Brahmanas. Resources came from **producers — peasants, cattle-keepers, artisans** — who had to give part of their produce as rent or revenue. Revenue collectors were often recruited from influential families; posts often became **hereditary**.

steps.title: Prashastis and land grants
steps.body: **Prashastis** were compositions praising rulers, written by learned Brahmanas. Kings rewarded Brahmanas with **grants of land**, recorded on **copper plates** given to the recipients. Kalhana's **Rajatarangini** (12th century, Kashmir) was a long Sanskrit poem on the history of Kashmir's kings; unusually, it was often critical of rulers.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why must historians be cautious with prashastis?

A: They were written to praise rulers, so they may exaggerate victories and qualities.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How was a land grant recorded? → On copper plates, which recorded the gift, the land's boundaries and the terms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking prashastis as plain facts.
- Thinking kings ruled alone — samantas and local associations shared power.

lessons.title: Warfare for wealth: Kanauj and raids

scenes.text: Kanauj, on the Ganga, was the most prized city of north India.
For centuries three dynasties fought over it.
Far to the north-west, a Sultan of Ghazni led raids to seize temple wealth.

steps.title: Tripartite struggle
steps.body: Rulers of the **Gurjara-Pratihara, Rashtrakuta and Pala** dynasties fought for control over **Kanauj** for centuries. Because three parties were involved, historians call it the **tripartite struggle**.

steps.title: Raids and temples
steps.body: Rulers displayed power by building large temples — so attacking an enemy's temple was also a show of power. **Mahmud of Ghazni** (ruled 997–1030, Afghanistan) raided the subcontinent **17 times**, targeting wealthy temples, including **Somnath** in Gujarat. Much of the wealth went to build a splendid capital at Ghazni. He sent the scholar **al-Biruni**, who wrote **Kitab al-Hind**, an account of the subcontinent, using Sanskrit scholars' help.

steps.title: Chahamanas (Chauhans)
steps.body: The **Chahamanas** ruled around Delhi and Ajmer. **Prithviraja III** defeated the Afghan ruler **Sultan Muhammad Ghori** in **1191**, but lost to him in **1192**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why did Mahmud of Ghazni attack temples?

A: Temples held great wealth, and attacking an enemy's temple also displayed power.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Which three dynasties fought the tripartite struggle and over what? → Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas, Palas — over Kanauj.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing 1191 (Prithviraja wins) and 1192 (Ghori wins).
- Thinking al-Biruni was a raider — he was a scholar.

events.text: Mahmud of Ghazni begins his rule

quiz.why: Three dynasties, the Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas, fought for control of Kanauj. This was the tripartite struggle.
Mahmud of Ghazni raided the subcontinent 17 times, mainly for wealth.
Kitab al-Hind was written by al-Biruni, a scholar who came with Mahmud's court.
Prithviraja III belonged to the Chahamana (Chauhan) dynasty.

quiz.q: Which temple did Mahmud of Ghazni raid?
quiz.why: Mahmud of Ghazni raided the Somnath temple in Gujarat, which was famous for its wealth.

lessons.title: The Cholas: kingdom, temples and villages

scenes.text: Visitors in Thanjavur gaze up at the towering Rajarajeshvara temple, built by the Chola king Rajaraja I.
Inside, exquisite bronze images of deities are carried in processions.
Around the temple lay fertile fields watered by the Kaveri, managed by village assemblies.

steps.title: Rise of the Cholas
steps.body: **Vijayalaya** of the Chola family of Uraiyur captured the Kaveri delta from the Muttaraiyar in the mid-9th century and built **Thanjavur** and a temple for goddess Nishumbhasudini. **Rajaraja I** (became king in 985) expanded control; his son **Rajendra I** raided the Ganga valley, Sri Lanka and countries of Southeast Asia, building a navy. He built **Gangaikondacholapuram**.

steps.title: Temples and bronze
steps.body: Big temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikondacholapuram were architectural and sculptural marvels. Temples were centres of settlements, craft production and economic, social and cultural life. They were endowed with land. Chola **bronze images** are among the finest in the world; most were of deities, sometimes of devotees, made by the lost-wax technique.

steps.title: Agriculture and irrigation
steps.body: The Kaveri delta's fertile soil supported agriculture. Embankments were built to prevent floods, canals carried water, wells were dug, and huge **tanks** collected rainwater. Many crops were grown twice a year.

steps.title: Administration and assemblies
steps.body: Settlements of peasants were called **ur**; groups of villages formed a **nadu**. Rich peasants of the Vellala caste exercised control. Brahmanas received land grants (**brahmadeya**); each was looked after by an assembly, the **sabha**, working through committees for irrigation, gardens, temples etc. Associations of traders were called **nagarams**. Inscriptions from **Uttaramerur** (Chingleput district) list rules for sabha membership: owning land from which revenue was collected, having one's own home, being 35–70 years old, knowledge of the Vedas, being honest; names were chosen by lottery for one-year terms.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Name four types of land in Chola inscriptions. → **Vellanvagai** (land of non-Brahmana peasant proprietors), **brahmadeya** (land gifted to Brahmanas), **shalabhoga** (land for maintenance of a school), **devadana / tirunamattukkani** (land gifted to temples), **pallichchhandam** (land donated to Jaina institutions).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing ur (village), nadu (group of villages), sabha (Brahmana assembly) and nagaram (traders' association).
- Thinking Chola bronze statues were cast in moulds reused many times — the lost-wax method breaks the mould each time.

Under the Cholas, the assembly of Brahmana landowners in a village was called a sabha. The traders' associations were nagarams.
The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe how the sabha was run, including rules for who could be a member.
Chola bronze images were made by the lost-wax technique. A wax model is covered in clay, the wax is melted out, and metal is poured in.

courses.title: Ch 3 · The Delhi Sultans (History)
courses.summary: How Delhi became a capital, the dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate from the early 13th century, sources like tawarikh, Raziyya Sultan, expansion from garrison towns, administration through iqtas, Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughluq, and the Sultanate in the 15th–16th centuries.
outcomes: Learners can name the dynasties and key rulers of the Delhi Sultanate in order
Learners can explain the sources (tawarikh) and their viewpoint
Learners can describe internal and external frontier expansion and the iqta system

lessons.title: Delhi becomes a capital; the dynasties

scenes.text: In Mehrauli, Delhi, Kabir stands beside the soaring Qutb Minar.
His guide explains: Delhi first became a capital under the Tomara Rajputs, then the Chauhans, then the Sultans.
For over 300 years, five dynasties of Sultans ruled from here.

steps.title: Delhi before the Sultans
steps.body: Delhi first became the capital of a kingdom under the **Tomara Rajputs**, who were defeated in the middle of the 12th century by the **Chauhans (Chahamanas)** of Ajmer. Under them Delhi became an important commercial centre; coins minted here, called **dehliwal**, circulated widely.

steps.title: Five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate
steps.body:
From the early 13th century:

- **Early Turkish rulers (1206–1290)**: Qutbuddin Aybak, Shamsuddin Iltutmish, Raziyya, Ghiyasuddin Balban
- **Khalji dynasty (1290–1320)**: Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin Khalji
- **Tughluq dynasty (1320–1414)**: Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, Muhammad Tughluq, Firuz Shah Tughluq
- **Sayyid dynasty (1414–1451)**: Khizr Khan
- **Lodi dynasty (1451–1526)**: Bahlul Lodi, Ibrahim Lodi

steps.title: Sources: tawarikh
steps.body: Histories (**tarikh**, plural **tawarikh**) were written in **Persian**, the language of administration. Authors were learned men — secretaries, administrators, poets, courtiers — who lived in cities (mainly Delhi), wrote for Sultans in the hope of rewards, and advised rulers on an ideal social order based on birthright and gender distinctions. Their ideas were not shared by everybody.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Arrange the dynasties: Lodi, Tughluq, Khalji, Sayyid, Early Turkish. → **Early Turkish → Khalji → Tughluq → Sayyid → Lodi**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why must we read tawarikh carefully?

A: Their authors wrote for Sultans, lived in cities, and held views favouring birthright and gender distinctions; they often ignored ordinary people's lives.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the Tughluqs before the Khaljis.
- Thinking tawarikh were neutral reports.

activity.prompt: Put the dynasties in order.

quiz.why: Delhi became a capital first under the Tomara Rajputs. The Chauhans later captured it.
Tawarikh, the histories of the Sultans, were written in Persian, the language of the court and administration.

quiz.q: Which dynasty came right after the Khaljis?
quiz.why: The Tughluqs followed the Khaljis in 1320. The Sayyids and Lodis came later, and the Mughals after them.

quiz.q: Coins minted in Delhi under the Chauhans
quiz.why: Coins minted in Delhi under the Tomaras and Chauhans were called dehliwal.
The Lodis (1451–1526) were the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.

lessons.title: Raziyya and the expansion of the Sultanate

story.title: A Sultan who was a daughter

scenes.text: In 1236, Sultan Iltutmish's daughter Raziyya became Sultan.
A chronicler admitted she was more able and qualified than her brothers…
…yet nobles disliked a woman ruling independently. She was removed in 1240.

steps.title: Raziyya Sultan (1236–1240)
steps.body: The chronicler **Minhaj-i Siraj** recognised her ability but was uncomfortable having a queen as ruler, as it went against the ideal social order. Nobles were unhappy with her attempts to rule independently, and she was removed from the throne in 1240.

steps.title: From garrison towns to empire
steps.body:
In the early 13th century, the Sultans' control rarely went beyond heavily fortified towns occupied by garrisons. They depended on trade, tribute or plunder for supplies.

- **Internal frontier**: consolidating the hinterlands of garrison towns — forests were cleared in the Ganga–Yamuna doab and land given to peasants; new fortresses and towns built.
- **External frontier**: military expeditions into southern India, starting under **Alauddin Khalji** and culminating with **Muhammad Tughluq**.

steps.title: Mosques
steps.body: Sultans built **mosques** in many cities to show they were protectors of Islam and Muslims. Examples: **Quwwat al-Islam** mosque (Delhi, late 12th century, enlarged by Iltutmish and Alauddin), Begumpuri mosque (built in Muhammad Tughluq's reign).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Distinguish the internal and external frontiers.

A: Internal: consolidating and settling the hinterlands near garrison towns. External: military campaigns far beyond, into southern India.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why was Raziyya removed? → Nobles opposed her independent rule as a woman, though she was able.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Sultans controlled all of India from 1206 — early control was limited to garrison towns.
- Confusing Raziyya's father (Iltutmish) with Balban.

statements.s: Raziyya ruled from 1236 to 1240.
Early Sultans controlled every village of the subcontinent.
Clearing forests in the doab was part of the internal frontier.
Campaigns into southern India began under Alauddin Khalji.
Mosques showed Sultans as protectors of Islam.

quiz.why: Raziyya was the daughter of Sultan Iltutmish and ruled after him from 1236 to 1240.
Garrison towns were fortified towns where soldiers were stationed to guard the Sultanate.

quiz.q: Expeditions into southern India form the
quiz.why: Campaigns into southern India took the Sultanate beyond its borders, so they were the external frontier.
The Quwwat al-Islam mosque is in Delhi, near the Qutb Minar.

quiz.q: Minhaj-i Siraj felt that a queen ruling
options: went against the ideal social order
quiz.why: Minhaj-i Siraj felt a queen ruling went against the ideal social order. This was his own view.

scenes.text: Iltutmish preferred to appoint his special slaves to high posts rather than powerful nobles.
These loyal men were given territories called iqtas to govern.
In return they collected revenue and kept soldiers ready for the Sultan.

steps.title: Bandagan and clients
steps.body: Early Delhi Sultans, especially **Iltutmish**, favoured their special slaves purchased for military service, called **bandagan** in Persian. They were carefully trained and totally dependent on their master, so the Sultan could trust them. The **Khaljis and Tughluqs** continued to use bandagan and also raised people of humble birth, often their **clients**, to high political positions. Nobles sometimes saw this as an insult.

steps.title: Iqtas and muqtis
steps.body: The Sultans assigned territories called **iqtas** to military commanders called **iqtadars** or **muqtis**. A muqti led military campaigns, maintained law and order in his iqta, and collected revenue to pay his soldiers. Under **Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad Tughluq**, control over muqtis was strengthened: accountants checked revenue records, and muqtis were often transferred so the post did not become hereditary.

steps.title: Taxes
steps.body: Three types: (1) on cultivation, **kharaj**, about **50% of the peasant's produce**; (2) on cattle; (3) on houses. Large parts of the subcontinent remained outside control — distant provinces like Bengal were hard to rule from Delhi; local chieftains resisted.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Why were bandagan trusted by the Sultans?

A: They were trained by and wholly dependent on the Sultan, so they owed him complete loyalty.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What were the duties of a muqti? → Lead military campaigns, maintain law and order in the iqta, collect revenue and pay soldiers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing iqta (territory) with muqti (holder).
- Thinking iqtas were permanent family property — Sultans tried to stop them becoming hereditary.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.
pairs: Special slaves trained for military service
Tax on cultivation (about half the produce)

quiz.why: Iqta holders were called muqtis. They collected revenue and kept soldiers.
Kharaj was a tax on cultivation, usually about half of the produce.
Bandagan were slaves trained for the army and administration. They were loyal to the Sultan.
Muqtis were moved around often so that their posts did not become hereditary and they could not grow too powerful.
Iltutmish favoured the bandagan, specially trained slaves who served him.

lessons.title: Alauddin Khalji, Muhammad Tughluq and after

scenes.text: Mongols under Genghis Khan's successors attacked north India in the 13th–14th centuries.
Alauddin Khalji built a garrison town, Siri, and controlled market prices to feed his huge army.
Muhammad Tughluq tried a different plan — moving the capital and issuing token coins. It went badly.

steps.title: Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316)
steps.body:
Faced Mongol invasions; defended Delhi.

- Raised a large **standing army**; built a new garrison town, **Siri**.
- Paid soldiers in **cash**, not iqtas.
- To feed soldiers, **controlled prices** of goods in Delhi; officials checked prices and punished merchants who did not sell at prescribed rates.
- Tax on produce fixed at 50%, collected in cash and kind.
His administrative measures were considered successful; he was praised for cheap prices and efficient supplies.

steps.title: Muhammad Tughluq (1324–1351)
steps.body:
- Defeated the Mongols, then planned to conquer Transoxiana and raised a large army.
- Shifted the population of Delhi (Dehli-i Kuhna) to **Daulatabad** in the Deccan, his second capital — causing great hardship; later many returned.
- Raised taxes in the doab at a time of **famine**, causing rebellion.
- Introduced **token currency** of cheap metal — people did not trust it and many forged coins; it had to be withdrawn.
Many of his measures failed.

steps.title: After the Tughluqs
steps.body: By 1400 the Sultanate had weakened (Timur's invasion of 1398 also damaged Delhi). Provinces like Jaunpur, Bengal, Malwa, Gujarat, Rajasthan and the south became independent. The **Afghan Sher Shah Sur (1540–1545)** started as a manager of his uncle's lands and challenged and defeated the Mughal emperor **Humayun**. He introduced an administration that **Akbar** later followed when he consolidated the Mughal Empire.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: Compare how Alauddin and Muhammad Tughluq paid soldiers and fed the army.

A: Alauddin paid in cash and controlled market prices in Delhi. Muhammad Tughluq also paid in cash but his heavy taxes during famine and token currency caused unrest.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why did token currency fail? → People did not trust coins made of cheap metal, and they could be easily forged.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing Siri (Alauddin) with Daulatabad (Muhammad Tughluq).
- Thinking Muhammad Tughluq's token currency was paper money — it was coins of cheap metal.

lessons.title: Who were the Mughals? Babur and Humayun

scenes.text: At 12, Babur became ruler of Ferghana in Central Asia, but was forced out by rivals.
He seized Kabul in 1504 and in 1526 defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat.
He captured Delhi and Agra — and the Mughal Empire began.

steps.title: Ancestry
steps.body: The Mughals descended from two great lineages: from their mother's side, **Genghis Khan** (Mongol ruler); from their father's side, **Timur** (ruler of Iran, Iraq and Turkey). They did not like to be called Mughal or Mongol, because of memories of Genghis Khan's massacres; they were proud of Timur, who had captured Delhi in 1398.

steps.title: Babur (1526–1530)
steps.body:
- **1526**: defeated Ibrahim Lodi and his Afghan supporters at **Panipat**, captured Delhi and Agra.
- **1527**: defeated **Rana Sanga**, Rajput rulers and allies at **Khanua**.
- 1528: defeated Rajputs at Chanderi; established control over Delhi and Agra before his death.

steps.title: Humayun (1530–1540, 1555–1556)
steps.body: Divided his inheritance as per his father's will among his brothers. **Sher Khan (Sher Shah)** defeated him at **Chausa (1539)** and **Kanauj (1540)**, forcing him to flee to Iran. With Safavid help he recaptured Delhi in **1555** but died the next year in an accident.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why were the Mughals proud of their Timurid ancestry? → Timur had captured Delhi in 1398; they celebrated their genealogy, and Mughal paintings showed Timur with them.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name the two battles in which Sher Khan defeated Humayun. → **Chausa (1539)** and **Kanauj (1540)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing Panipat 1526 (Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi) with Khanua 1527 (Babur vs Rana Sanga).
- Thinking Humayun ruled continuously — he lost the throne for 15 years.

After losing to Sher Khan, Humayun took refuge at the Safavid court in Iran.
Sher Khan defeated Humayun at Chausa in 1539 and again at Kanauj.

scenes.text: Akbar became emperor at just 13 years old in 1556.
Over the next fifty years he expanded the empire from Kabul to Bengal and into the Deccan.
His court historian Abul Fazl recorded his reign in the Akbar Nama.

steps.title: Akbar (1556–1605)
steps.body:
- 1556–1570: became independent of his regent **Bairam Khan**; campaigns against the Suris and Afghans, against Malwa and Gondwana, and the Sisodiyas of Mewar (Chittor captured 1568, Ranthambhor 1569).
- 1570–1585: campaigns in Gujarat, then in Bihar, Bengal and Orissa (complicated by a 1579–80 revolt).
- 1585–1605: expansion to Kabul, Kashmir, Qandahar; then the Deccan (Berar, Khandesh, parts of Ahmadnagar).

steps.title: Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb
steps.body:
- **Jahangir (1605–1627)**: continued Akbar's campaigns; the Sisodiya ruler of Mewar, Amar Singh, accepted Mughal service.
- **Shah Jahan (1627–1658)**: campaigns in the Deccan; Ahmadnagar annexed; built many monuments.
- **Aurangzeb (1658–1707)**: long campaigns in the Deccan; annexed Bijapur (1685) and Golconda (1687). After 1698 he personally campaigned against the **Marathas** using guerrilla warfare. Rebellions by Sikhs, Jats and Satnamis; Maratha leader **Shivaji** carved out an independent state.

steps.title: Succession and other rulers
steps.body: Mughals did not follow primogeniture (eldest son inherits). They followed the Timurid custom of **coparcenary inheritance** — division among all sons — so princes often fought for the throne. Mughals **married into Rajput families** (e.g. Jahangir's mother was a Kachhwaha princess of Amber) and gave Rajputs high positions; the Sisodiya Rajputs long refused to accept Mughal authority. Defeated rulers were usually given back their lands as **watan jagir** (assignment) with honour.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why did Mughal succession often lead to war? → Coparcenary inheritance divided the inheritance among sons; there was no fixed rule that the eldest inherits, so brothers competed.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How did marriage alliances help the Mughals? → They built ties with Rajput families, who served as commanders and mansabdars.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking all Rajputs allied with the Mughals — the Sisodiyas of Mewar long resisted.
- Mixing Jahangir's and Shah Jahan's order: Akbar → Jahangir → Shah Jahan → Aurangzeb.

He must keep a specified number of cavalrymen for the emperor.
He is paid by the revenue of an assignment of land, a jagir.

steps.title: Mansabdars
steps.body: As the empire grew, the Mughals recruited diverse people: Turani and Irani nobles, Rajputs, Afghans, Ethiopians, Indian Muslims, Marathas. A **mansabdar** was an individual holding a **mansab** (position or rank). Rank was shown by a number called **zat**: the higher the zat, the more prestigious the noble and the larger his salary. Mansabdars also had to maintain a specified number of **sawar** (cavalrymen).

steps.title: Jagirs
steps.body: Mansabdars received salaries as revenue assignments called **jagirs** (somewhat like iqtas). Unlike muqtis, most mansabdars did not live in or administer their jagirs; they only had rights to revenue, collected by their servants. In Akbar's reign jagirs were carefully assessed; under Aurangzeb, the number of mansabdars grew, there was a shortage of jagirs, and jagirdars tried to extract as much as possible — peasants suffered.

steps.title: Zabt and zamindars
steps.body: The main source of income was taxes on peasants' produce. Usually, taxes were paid through rural elites — the headman or local chieftain — called **zamindars**. Akbar's revenue minister **Todar Mal** carried out a careful survey of crop yields, prices and areas cultivated for a 10-year period (1570–1580). Tax was fixed on each crop in cash. Each province was divided into revenue circles with its own schedule of revenue rates. This system was called **zabt**; it was used where Mughal officials could survey land carefully (not in Gujarat and Bengal).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What does 'zat 7000' indicate? → A very high rank, more prestige and a larger salary for that mansabdar.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: Why did peasants suffer in Aurangzeb's later years?

A: There were many mansabdars and too few jagirs; jagirdars squeezed as much revenue as possible during their short tenure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking mansabdars governed their jagirs like muqtis governed iqtas.
- Confusing Todar Mal's survey (zabt) with the price control of Alauddin Khalji.
