lessons.title: Akbar's policies and the empire later

scenes.text: At Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar built the ibadat khana, a house of worship for discussions.
Scholars — ulama, Brahmanas, Jesuit priests from Goa, Zoroastrians — debated there.
From these talks grew his idea of sulh-i kul: universal peace.

steps.title: Administration
steps.body: The empire was divided into provinces called **subas**, governed by a **subadar**, who had both political and military functions. Each province also had a financial officer, **diwan**. Other officers: **bakhshi** (military paymaster), **sadr** (in charge of religious and charitable patronage), **faujdars** (military commanders), **kotwal** (town police commander).

steps.title: Sulh-i kul
steps.body: Akbar's interaction with people of different faiths made him realise that religious scholars who emphasised ritual and dogma were often bigots. He developed **sulh-i kul**, or **universal peace**: tolerance did not discriminate between people of different religions; it focused on a system of ethics — honesty, justice, peace — applicable everywhere. **Abul Fazl** helped frame this vision. Jahangir and Shah Jahan followed this principle too.

steps.title: The 17th century and after
steps.body: Mughal administrative and military efficiency brought economic and commercial prosperity, while poverty remained for many. By the late 17th century, the authority of the Mughal emperor slowly declined; mansabdars and subadars built independent dynasties and new states emerged in the 18th century.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What was the role of the ibadat khana? → A hall at Fatehpur Sikri where Akbar held discussions with scholars of many faiths.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Q: How was sulh-i kul different from mere tolerance of other religions?

A: It was an ethical system — honesty, justice, peace — applied to everyone regardless of religion, not just permission to follow different faiths.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling sulh-i kul a new religion. It was a principle of governance.
- Mixing subadar (governor) with diwan (finance).

courses.title: Ch 5 · Tribes, Nomads and Settled Communities (History)
courses.summary: Societies beyond the big cities and courts: tribes and their ways of life, nomadic pastoralists and trading Banjaras, the rise of new castes, and the tribal kingdoms of the Gonds and Ahoms.
outcomes: Learners can explain how tribal societies differed from varna-based societies
Learners can describe the lives of nomadic pastoralists and Banjaras
Learners can explain how new jatis and Rajput clans emerged
Learners can describe the Gond and Ahom states
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: While Sultans and Mughals ruled cities, many people lived in forests, hills and deserts.
They followed customs passed down through generations and owned land jointly as a clan.
These tribes were spread across the whole subcontinent.

steps.title: Tribal society
steps.body: In varna-based society, Brahmanas ranked people and inequalities grew. But many societies did not follow varna rules — the **tribes**. Members were united by **kinship bonds**. Many lived by agriculture; others were hunter-gatherers or herders, or combined these. Many were nomadic. A tribe jointly controlled land and pastures and divided it among households by its own rules.

steps.title: Some tribes and regions
steps.body:
- **Khokhar** (13th–14th c.) and later **Gakkhar** — Punjab (Kamal Khan Gakkhar became a Mughal noble under Akbar)
- **Langahs and Arghuns** — Multan and Sind
- **Balochis** — north-west
- **Gaddis** — shepherds of the western Himalaya
- **Nagas, Ahoms** and others — north-east
- **Cheros** (Bihar–Jharkhand), **Mundas and Santals** (Jharkhand, Orissa, Bengal)
- **Kolis, Berads** — Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat
- **Bhils** — western and central India
- **Gonds** — Chhattisgarh, MP, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Q: How did a tribe hold land?

A: The tribe as a whole controlled land and pastures and divided them among households according to its own customs.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name a tribe each from Punjab, the north-east and central India. → Gakkhar (Punjab), Ahom/Naga (north-east), Gond (central India).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking tribes were all hunter-gatherers; many were farmers or herders.
- Thinking tribal societies wrote chronicles like courts — most preserved history orally.

scenes.text: A long caravan of oxen loaded with grain winds along a dusty road.
The Banjaras buy grain in villages and carry it to towns and army camps.
Even the army of Alauddin Khalji depended on such carriers for supplies.

steps.title: Nomadic pastoralists
steps.body: **Nomadic pastoralists** moved over long distances with their animals. They lived on milk and other pastoral products and exchanged wool, ghee etc. with settled agriculturists for grain, cloth, utensils. Some carried goods from place to place on animals.

steps.title: Banjaras
steps.body: The **Banjaras** were the most important trader-nomads. Their caravan was called a **tanda**. **Sultan Alauddin Khalji** used Banjaras to transport grain to city markets. Emperor **Jahangir** wrote that Banjaras carried grain on bullocks from different areas and sold it in towns; they transported food grain for the Mughal army during campaigns — large armies could need 100 000 bullocks.

steps.title: Changing society: new castes
steps.body: As the economy and society grew, people needed new skills — smiths, carpenters, masons. Among varna-based groups, smaller castes or **jatis** emerged, recognised as separate. Jatis, rather than varna, became the basis for organising society. Among Kshatriyas, new **Rajput clans** became powerful (Hunas, Chandelas, Chalukyas…). Many tribes became part of caste-based society, but only leading families joined the ruling class.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why were Banjaras important to armies? → They transported large quantities of grain to feed soldiers during campaigns.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why did new jatis emerge? → New occupations arose as the economy grew; groups following them came to be seen as separate jatis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing tanda (Banjara caravan) with garh (Gond unit).
- Thinking nomads had no links with settled people — they traded regularly.

story.title: The queen who would not surrender

scenes.text: Rani Durgawati ruled the Gond kingdom of Garha Katanga after her husband's death.
In 1565, Mughal forces under Asaf Khan attacked.
She fought bravely but was defeated; she chose death rather than surrender.

steps.title: Gond country
steps.body: The **Gonds** lived in a vast forested region called **Gondwana** ('country inhabited by Gonds'). They practised **shifting cultivation**. The large Gond tribe was divided into many smaller clans, each with its own raja or rai.

steps.title: Administration of Gond kingdoms
steps.body: As the Delhi Sultans' power declined, a few large Gond kingdoms began to dominate smaller chiefs. The **Akbar Nama** mentions the Gond kingdom of **Garha Katanga** with 70 000 villages. Its administration was centralised: the kingdom was divided into **garhs**, each controlled by a particular Gond clan. A garh was further divided into units of **84 villages** called **chaurasi**, and a chaurasi into **barhots** of **12 villages** each.

steps.title: Change and conquest
steps.body: As states emerged, Gond society changed: basically equal society gradually divided into unequal classes; Brahmanas received land grants and became influential; Gond chiefs wished to be recognised as Rajputs. Garha Katanga was rich — it traded wild elephants to other kingdoms. In **1565** the Mughals under **Asaf Khan** defeated **Rani Durgawati**. Though defeated, Garha Katanga continued for some time, and the Gonds kept their identity.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How was the Gond kingdom divided? → Kingdom → garhs (controlled by clans) → chaurasi (84 villages) → barhot (12 villages).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why was Garha Katanga wealthy? → It traded in wild elephants and other goods, and controlled many villages.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing chaurasi (84 villages) and barhot (12 villages).
- Thinking Gonds became extinct after 1565 — they survive as a large community today.

scenes.text: In the 13th century, the Ahoms migrated from present-day Myanmar into the Brahmaputra valley.
They built a new state, suppressing the older landlords (bhuiyans).
Their historians wrote detailed chronicles called buranjis.

steps.title: The Ahom state
steps.body: The **Ahoms** created a new state by suppressing the older political system of the **bhuiyans** (landlords). During the 16th century they annexed the kingdoms of the **Chhutiyas (1523)** and **Koch-Hajo (1581)** and subjugated many other tribes. They built a large state and used **firearms** as early as the 1530s; by the 1660s they could make high-quality gunpowder and cannons.

steps.title: Paiks and administration
steps.body: The Ahom state depended on **forced labour**. Those forced to work for the state were called **paiks**. A census of the population was taken; each village had to send a number of paiks by rotation. People from heavily populated areas were shifted to less populated places, breaking Ahom clans. By the first half of the 17th century the administration was quite centralised. Almost all adult males served in the army in times of war.

steps.title: Society and culture
steps.body: Ahom society was divided into clans called **khels**; a khel often controlled several villages. Peasants were given land by their village community. Earlier Ahoms worshipped tribal gods; in the first half of the 17th century, Brahmanas' influence increased and Hinduism became predominant, but Ahom kings did not completely give up traditional beliefs. Poets and scholars were given land grants; theatre was encouraged; Sanskrit works were translated into local languages. Historical works (**buranjis**) were written first in Ahom and then in Assamese.

steps.title: Mughal attack
steps.body: In **1662** the Mughals under **Mir Jumla** attacked and defeated the Ahoms, but their direct control over the region did not last long.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Who were paiks? → People who were forced to work for the Ahom state (by rotation from each village).

- Thinking the Mughals ruled Assam permanently after 1662.

lessons.title: The idea of bhakti; Nayanars and Alvars

scenes.text: In a Tamil temple town, singers perform hymns written over a thousand years ago.
Their composers came from many castes — potters, farmers, hunters, even "untouchables".
They sang that God is reached through love, not birth or ritual.

steps.title: A supreme god and bhakti
steps.body: Earlier, people worshipped many gods. Gradually ideas of a supreme god who could deliver humans from bondage (the cycle of birth and rebirth) through **devotion** (bhakti) became popular. The **Bhagavad Gita** had popularised the idea of devotion to a personal god; Shiva, Vishnu and Durga became supreme deities worshipped through elaborate rituals.

steps.title: Nayanars and Alvars (7th–9th centuries)
steps.body:
In south India, new religious movements were led by the **Nayanars** (saints devoted to **Shiva**) and **Alvars** (saints devoted to **Vishnu**). They came from all castes, including those considered 'untouchable' like the Pulaiyar and Panars. They criticised Buddhists and Jainas and preached ardent love of Shiva or Vishnu. They drew on Sangam literature ideals of love and heroism.

- There were **63 Nayanars** (Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar, Manikkavasagar); their songs form the **Tevaram** and **Tiruvacakam**.
- There were **12 Alvars** (Periyalvar, his daughter Andal, Tondaradippodi Alvar, Nammalvar); their songs were compiled in the **Divya Prabandham**.

Chola and Pandya kings built elaborate temples around shrines visited by saint-poets.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Distinguish Nayanars from Alvars. → Nayanars: devotees of Shiva (63). Alvars: devotees of Vishnu (12).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What was new about these saints' message? → They taught that anyone, of any caste, could reach God through love and devotion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the deities: Nayanar–Shiva, Alvar–Vishnu.
- Thinking bhakti saints were only Brahmanas.

activity.prompt: Nayanar or Alvar?

quiz.why: The Nayanars were devotees of Shiva. The Alvars were devotees of Vishnu.
There were 12 Alvars, and 63 Nayanars. The number 108 is not used for them.

quiz.q: Divya Prabandham contains songs of the
quiz.why: The Divya Prabandham is a collection of the songs of the Alvars, who were devotees of Vishnu.

quiz.q: Bhakti saints of the south came from
quiz.why: The bhakti saints of the south came from all castes, including those considered low. Many were not Brahmanas.
Andal was a woman Alvar saint. Her songs are still sung today.

lessons.title: Philosophers and movements: Shankara to Maharashtra

scenes.text: In 8th-century Kerala, Shankara taught that the soul and the supreme god are one.
In 11th-century Tamil Nadu, Ramanuja taught that the soul, though united with God, stays distinct.
Their ideas shaped devotion across India for centuries.

steps.title: Shankara and Ramanuja
steps.body:
- **Shankara** (born in Kerala, 8th century): advocate of **Advaita** — the oneness of the individual soul and the Supreme God (Brahman), the Ultimate Reality, which is formless and without attributes. He considered the world an illusion (maya), preached renunciation and the path of knowledge.
- **Ramanuja** (born in Tamil Nadu, 11th century): influenced by the Alvars; the best means of salvation is intense devotion to Vishnu. He propounded **Vishishtadvaita** — qualified oneness: the soul, even when united with the Supreme God, remains distinct.

steps.title: Basavanna's Virashaivism
steps.body: In Karnataka in the mid-12th century, **Basavanna** and companions Allama Prabhu and Akkamahadevi started the **Virashaiva** movement. They argued for equality of all human beings and against Brahmanical ideas about caste and the treatment of women; they were against rituals and idol worship.

steps.title: Saints of Maharashtra
steps.body: From the 13th to 17th centuries: **Jnaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram**, and women like **Sakhubai**, as well as the family of **Chokhamela**, of the 'untouchable' Mahar caste. This regional tradition focused on the **Vitthala** (a form of Vishnu) temple in **Pandharpur**, and on the idea of a personal god residing in people's hearts. They rejected ritualism, outward displays of piety and caste differences; they even rejected renunciation, preferring to live with family, earning a living and serving fellow humans.

steps.title: Nathpanthis, Siddhas and Yogis
steps.body: They criticised ritual and the social order, advocated renunciation of the world, and believed the path to salvation lay in meditation on the formless Ultimate Reality, using yogasanas, breathing exercises and meditation. They were popular among 'low' castes.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Compare Advaita and Vishishtadvaita. → Advaita: soul and God are one (Shankara). Vishishtadvaita: soul united with God remains distinct (Ramanuja).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the regions: Shankara – Kerala; Ramanuja – Tamil Nadu; Basavanna – Karnataka; Vitthala – Pandharpur, Maharashtra.
- Thinking Maharashtra's saints asked people to give up family life — they did not.

scenes.text: On a Thursday evening at the dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi, qawwals sing.
People of every faith sit together listening.
Sufi saints taught love of God and compassion for all — the same spirit as bhakti.

steps.title: Who were the Sufis?
steps.body: **Sufis** were Muslim mystics. They rejected outward religiosity and emphasised **love and devotion to God** and **compassion towards all fellow human beings**. Islam propagated strict monotheism (submission to one God) and rejected idol worship; it simplified rituals. Sufis often rejected elaborate rituals and codes of behaviour demanded by Muslim religious scholars. They sought union with God much as a lover seeks the beloved, with total disregard for the world. Like the saint-poets, Sufis composed poems.

steps.title: Practices and silsilas
steps.body: Sufis developed methods of training using **zikr** (chanting of a name or sacred formula), contemplation, **sama** (singing), **raqs** (dancing), discussion of parables, breath control etc., under the guidance of a master or **pir**. Thus arose the **silsilas** — a genealogy of Sufi teachers. Masters held assemblies in their **khanqahs** (hospices); devotees of all backgrounds came. The tomb of a Sufi saint, the **dargah**, became a place of pilgrimage.

steps.title: Chishti silsila
steps.body: Most influential in the 12th century and after. Masters: **Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti** of **Ajmer**, **Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki** of **Delhi**, **Baba Farid** of **Punjab**, **Khwaja Nizamuddin Auliya** of **Delhi** and **Bandanawaz Gisudaraz** of **Gulbarga**. Central Asia's great Sufis included Ghazzali, Rumi and Sadi.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What is the difference between a khanqah and a dargah? → Khanqah: hospice where a Sufi master taught and met devotees. Dargah: the tomb of a Sufi saint, a place of pilgrimage.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name the Chishti saint of Ajmer. → **Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Sufis were only for Muslims — people of many faiths visited them.
- Confusing pir (master) and murid (disciple).

A Sufi hospice, where a teacher lived with his disciples, was called a khanqah.

quiz.q: Chanting a name or sacred formula
quiz.why: Zikr is the chanting of a name or sacred formula. Sama is Sufi singing.
A silsila is the chain or lineage of Sufi teachers and their disciples, from one master to the next.
A dargah is the tomb of a Sufi saint. A khanqah is a hospice.

lessons.title: Kabir, Guru Nanak and other saints of north India

scenes.text: In 15th-century Benares, Kabir, a weaver, sang couplets that everyone could understand.
He mocked empty rituals of both Hindus and Muslims and spoke of a formless Supreme God.
Some of his verses are found in the Guru Granth Sahib.

steps.title: Kabir (15th–16th centuries)
steps.body: Brought up in a family of Muslim **julahas** (weavers) near Benares (Varanasi). His ideas survive in sakhis and pads, sung by wandering singers; some were later collected in the Guru Granth Sahib, Panch Vani and Bijak. He **rejected major religious traditions' external worship**, the caste system and priestly authority. He believed in a formless Supreme God (Rama/Allah/Hari names for the same) and preached that bhakti was the only path to salvation. His language was spoken Hindi, easily understood by ordinary people.

steps.title: Guru Nanak (1469–1539)
steps.body: Born at **Talwandi** (Nankana Sahib, Pakistan). Travelled widely, then established a centre at **Kartarpur** (Dera Baba Nanak on the river Ravi). A **common kitchen (langar)** was organised where people ate together irrespective of caste or creed. The sacred space was called **dharmsal** (now **gurdwara**). Before his death he appointed **Lehna** (Guru Angad) as successor. **Guru Arjan** compiled the compositions of the first five Gurus and of others like Baba Farid, Ravidas and Kabir in the **Adi Granth Sahib** (1604). **Guru Gobind Singh** added his father Guru Tegh Bahadur's compositions; it became the **Guru Granth Sahib**. Guru Nanak's message: worship of one God, **nam** (right worship), **dan** (welfare of others), **isnan** (purity of conduct) — **nam japna, kirt karna, vand chhakna** (meditate on the name, work hard, share earnings). He taught equality.

steps.title: Mirabai and other saints
steps.body:
- **Mirabai**: a Rajput princess married into the royal family of Mewar in the 16th century; disciple of **Ravidas** (considered 'untouchable'); devoted to **Krishna**; her bhajans challenged norms of the 'upper' castes.
- **Surdas** (devotee of Krishna): Sursagara, Surasaravali.
- **Tulsidas**: wrote the **Ramcharitmanas** in **Awadhi**.
- **Shankaradeva** of **Assam** (late 15th c.): devotion to Vishnu; set up **namghars** (houses of recitation and prayer).
- **Chaitanyadeva** in Bengal; Dadu Dayal, Ravidas.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: State three teachings of Guru Nanak. → Worship of one God, equality irrespective of caste/creed/gender, and nam japna, kirt karna, vand chhakna (right worship, honest work, sharing).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Guru Granth Sahib contains only the Gurus' writings — it also includes Kabir, Baba Farid and others.
- Mixing Tulsidas (Awadhi Ramcharitmanas) and Surdas (Krishna).

lessons.title: Language and region: the Cheras and Malayalam

scenes.text: A 14th-century grammar book from Kerala describes a style of writing called "Manipravalam".
It means "diamonds and corals" — Sanskrit and the local language woven together.
Kerala's Chera rulers had already used Malayalam in inscriptions centuries earlier.

steps.title: Regions are made by mixing
steps.body: We often identify regions by language — Tamil Nadu with Tamil, Gujarat with Gujarati — but regional cultures grew through the **intermixing of local traditions with ideas from other parts of the subcontinent**.

steps.title: The Cheras and Malayalam
steps.body: The **Chera kingdom of Mahodayapuram** was established in the **9th century** in the south-western part of the peninsula, part of present-day Kerala. The rulers introduced the **Malayalam** language and script in their inscriptions — among the earliest examples of a regional language in official records. They also drew on Sanskritic traditions; temple theatre of Kerala borrowed stories from Sanskrit epics. The first literary works in Malayalam (around the 12th century) are directly indebted to Sanskrit. A 14th-century text, the **Lilatilakam**, dealing with grammar and poetics, was composed in **Manipravalam** — 'diamonds and corals', referring to Sanskrit and the regional language.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What does Manipravalam mean and what does it show? → 'Diamonds and corals'; it shows Sanskrit and Malayalam being used together — local and wider traditions mixing.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why are Chera inscriptions important? → They are among the earliest uses of a regional language (Malayalam) in official records.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking regional cultures developed in isolation.
- Confusing the Cheras (Kerala) with the Cholas (Tamil Nadu).

lessons.title: Rulers and religious traditions: Jagannatha; Rajputs and heroes

scenes.text: Every year in Puri, Odisha, huge chariots carry images of Jagannatha through the streets.
The main image is made of wood, as in local tribal traditions.
In the 13th century, a king even dedicated his whole kingdom to this deity.

steps.title: The Jagannatha cult
steps.body: In Puri, local people made a wooden image of the deity, suggesting he was originally a **local tribal god**; later identified with **Vishnu**. In the **12th century**, **Anantavarman**, a ruler of the **Ganga dynasty**, decided to build a temple for Purushottama Jagannatha at Puri. In **1230**, King **Anangabhima III** dedicated his kingdom to the deity and called himself the 'deputy' of the god. As the temple grew in importance, conquerors (Mughals, Marathas, the English East India Company) tried to control it, hoping this would make their rule acceptable to local people.

steps.title: Rajputs and heroic traditions
steps.body: In the 19th century, the region of most of present-day Rajasthan was called **Rajputana** by the British. Rajput rulers cherished the ideal of the **hero who fought valiantly**, often choosing death on the battlefield rather than defeat. Stories of Rajput heroes (like **Prithviraj**) were recorded in poems and songs recited by specially trained minstrels. Women sometimes followed their husbands in death — the practice of **sati** (self-immolation of widows); this must be understood critically, as women had no real choice.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why did conquerors try to control the Jagannatha temple? → It was an important pilgrimage centre; control could win the acceptance of local people and its wealth.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How were Rajput heroic stories preserved? → In poems and songs recited by trained minstrels.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the Jagannatha image is stone; it is wooden.
- Presenting sati as heroic — historians see it as a cruel social practice; it was later abolished by law.

scenes.text: A Kathak dancer spins rapidly, ankle bells ringing in perfect rhythm.
In a museum nearby, palm-sized paintings show Krishna with gopis in fine detail.
Both arts were shaped in temples and royal courts over centuries.

steps.title: Kathak
steps.body: **Kathak** comes from *katha*, a word used in Sanskrit and other languages for story. **Kathaks** were originally a caste of **storytellers in temples of north India**, who embellished performances with gestures and songs. From the 15th–16th centuries, with the spread of bhakti, Kathak evolved into a distinct dance form; legends of **Radha–Krishna** were enacted in folk plays called **rasa lila**. Under the Mughals, it was performed in courts, acquiring its present features. It developed in two traditions (**gharanas**): in the courts of **Rajasthan (Jaipur)** and **Lucknow**. Under **Wajid Ali Shah**, the last Nawab of Awadh, it grew into a major art form. In the 20th century, after independence, it was recognised as one of the **classical** dance forms of the country (others include Bharatanatyam, Kathakali, Odissi, Kuchipudi and Manipuri).

steps.title: Miniature painting
steps.body: **Miniatures** are small paintings, generally in watercolour on cloth or paper. The earliest were on palm leaves or wood. The **Mughal** emperors Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan patronised highly skilled painters who illustrated histories and poetry, often with court scenes, battles, hunting. With the decline of the Mughal Empire, painters moved to regional courts; in Rajasthan (Mewar, Jodhpur, Bundi, Kota, Kishangarh) they depicted mythology and poetry. In the Himalayan foothills, a bold style called **Basohli** developed; after **Nadir Shah's invasion (1739)** Mughal artists moved to the hills, founding the **Kangra** school, inspired by Vaishnavite traditions and soft colours. Ordinary people also painted on pots, walls, floors and cloth.

steps.title: Solved example 2

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Thinking Kathak began in Mughal courts — it began with temple storytellers.
- Mixing Basohli (bold style) and Kangra (soft colours).

scenes.text: In Kolkata, Rimi's family eats rice and fish curry almost every day.
On a trip to Bishnupur she sees temples with sloping roofs like village huts, covered in terracotta tiles.
Bengal's language, food, faith and buildings all have long histories.

steps.title: Growth of Bengali
steps.body: Bengali is now recognised as a language derived from **Sanskrit**, but early Sanskrit texts suggest people of Bengal did not speak Sanskritic languages. From the 4th–3rd centuries BCE, commercial ties with Magadha led to the growth of Sanskrit there. In the 7th century, Chinese traveller **Xuan Zang** noted languages related to Sanskrit in use across Bengal. From the 8th century, Bengal was ruled by the Palas; from the 14th to 16th centuries by Sultans independent of Delhi; in 1586, when Akbar conquered Bengal, it became the core of the **Bengal suba**. Persian was the language of administration, but Bengali developed as a regional language. Early Bengali literature: (1) works indebted to Sanskrit — Mangalakavyas, bhakti literature such as biographies of **Chaitanyadeva**; (2) Nath literature — songs of Maynamati and Gopichandra, stories of Dharma Thakur, fairy tales, folk tales, ballads.

steps.title: Pirs and temples
steps.body: From the 16th century, people migrated from western Bengal to the forested, swampy south-east, clearing land for rice. Community leaders who functioned as teachers and adjudicators, sometimes believed to have supernatural powers, were called **pirs** (including saints, Sufis, and even Hindu deities and spirits). Temple building took off in the late 15th century; many modest temples were built of brick and terracotta, with roofs copying thatched huts: **dochala** (two-roofed) and **chauchala** (four-roofed). Temples at **Bishnupur** are famous; outer walls were decorated with paintings, ornamental tiles or terracotta tablets.

steps.title: Fish as food
steps.body: Bengal is a riverine plain producing plenty of rice and fish — the traditional diet. Fishing was an important occupation. Terracotta temple walls depict fish. Though Brahmanas were not allowed non-vegetarian food, the popularity of fish made Brahmanical authorities relax the rule; the **Brihaddharma Purana**, a 13th-century Sanskrit text from Bengal, permitted local Brahmanas to eat certain varieties of fish.

steps.title: Solved example 1

scenes.text: In 1739, Nadir Shah of Iran sacked Delhi and carried away enormous wealth, including the Peacock Throne.
The once-mighty Mughal Empire could not stop him.
By the mid-18th century, new states had risen all over the subcontinent.

steps.title: Causes of crisis
steps.body:
- **Aurangzeb** had depleted military and financial resources by fighting a long war in the **Deccan**.
- Under his successors, administration broke down; it became difficult for later emperors to control powerful mansabdars.
- Nobles appointed as governors (**subadars**) controlled revenue and military offices, gaining great power.
- Peasant and zamindari **rebellions** in many parts of north and western India.
- Revenue resources shifted to provincial governors, local chieftains and other groups.

steps.title: Invasions
steps.body:
- **Nadir Shah** of Iran **sacked Delhi in 1739** and took away immense wealth.
- **Ahmad Shah Abdali** of Afghanistan invaded north India **five times between 1748 and 1761**.
- The Third Battle of Panipat (**1761**) — Abdali defeated the Marathas.

The empire was further weakened by competition among groups of nobles — the **Iranis and Turanis**. Two Mughal emperors (Farrukh Siyar 1713–1719 and Alamgir II 1754–1759) were assassinated, and two others (Ahmad Shah and Shah Alam II) were blinded by their nobles.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Give two reasons for the decline of the Mughal Empire. → Long Deccan wars under Aurangzeb drained resources; later emperors could not control powerful nobles and subadars.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Who invaded north India five times between 1748 and 1761? → **Ahmad Shah Abdali**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing Nadir Shah (Iran, 1739) with Ahmad Shah Abdali (Afghanistan, 1748–1761).
- Thinking the Mughal Empire ended in 1707 — it weakened but continued formally until 1857.

lessons.title: New states: Hyderabad, Awadh and Bengal

scenes.text: Three powerful Mughal nobles — in Hyderabad, Awadh and Bengal — still sent gifts to Delhi.
But they kept the revenue, appointed their own officials and passed power to their sons.
In practice they had become independent rulers.

steps.title: Hyderabad
steps.body: **Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah**, one of the most powerful members of Farrukh Siyar's court, was entrusted with the governorship of the Deccan. He founded Hyderabad state (**1724**), brought skilled soldiers and administrators from northern India, appointed mansabdars and granted jagirs. Though still a Mughal servant, he ruled independently without seeking Delhi's direction. The state constantly fought the Marathas to the west and the independent Telugu warrior chiefs (**nayakas**) of the plateau.

steps.title: Awadh
steps.body: **Burhan-ul-Mulk Sa'adat Khan** was appointed subadar of Awadh in **1722**. Awadh was prosperous, controlling the rich alluvial Ganga plain and the main trade route between north India and Bengal. He held the combined offices of subadari, diwani and faujdari, reduced the number of Mughal-appointed office holders, reduced jagirs, and depended on **revenue farmers** (ijaradars) — bankers and others who agreed to pay the state a fixed sum, raising their influence.

steps.title: Bengal
steps.body: Under **Murshid Quli Khan** (appointed naib/deputy to the governor), Bengal gradually broke away from Mughal control. He transferred all Mughal jagirdars to Orissa and ordered a major reassessment of Bengal's revenues, collected in cash with great strictness from zamindars. Many zamindars had to borrow from bankers. Under **Alivardi Khan** (r. 1740–1756), the banking house of **Jagat Seth** became extremely prosperous.

steps.title: Common features
steps.body: In all three states: (1) many of the older Mughal methods were continued, but **jagirdari was reduced** and (2) **revenue farming** (ijaradari) was used; (3) they built relationships with bankers and merchants, who lent money and gained influence.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What was ijaradari? → Revenue farming: the state let a contractor (ijaradar) collect taxes in return for a fixed sum paid to the state.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking these rulers openly rejected the Mughal emperor — they formally accepted him but ruled independently.
- Mixing founders: Hyderabad — Asaf Jah; Awadh — Sa'adat Khan; Bengal — Murshid Quli Khan.

scenes.text: On Baisakhi in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa.
The Khalsa fought for justice; after his death, Banda Bahadur led them against Mughal authority.
A century later, Maharaja Ranjit Singh ruled from Lahore.

steps.title: The Rajputs
steps.body: Many Rajput kings, especially of **Amber** and **Jodhpur**, had served the Mughals with distinction. In the 18th century they tried to extend control over adjacent regions. **Ajit Singh** of Jodhpur was involved in Mughal court factional politics. Influential Rajput families claimed subadari of the rich provinces of Gujarat and Malwa. **Raja Jai Singh** of Amber, governor of Malwa, founded his new capital at **Jaipur**; he was given subadari of Agra in 1722. Maratha campaigns into Rajasthan from the 1740s put pressure on these principalities.

steps.title: The Sikhs
steps.body: Organisation of the Sikhs into a political community in the 17th century helped regional state-building in Punjab. Several battles were fought by **Guru Gobind Singh** against Rajput and Mughal rulers before and after he instituted the **Khalsa in 1699**. After his death in 1708, the Khalsa rose in revolt against Mughal authority under **Banda Bahadur**'s leadership, declared their sovereign rule by striking coins in the name of Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh, and set up their own administration between the Sutlej and the Jamuna. Banda Bahadur was captured in **1715** and executed in **1716**.

steps.title: Misls and Ranjit Singh
steps.body: In the 18th century, the Sikhs organised into bands called **jathas**, and later **misls**. Their combined forces were the grand army (**dal khalsa**). The dal khalsa met at **Amritsar** at Baisakhi and Diwali to take collective decisions, called **gurmatas**. A system called **rakhi** was introduced, offering protection to cultivators for a tax of **20% of the produce**. The Khalsa resisted the Mughals and Ahmad Shah Abdali. **Maharaja Ranjit Singh** reunited the groups and established his capital at **Lahore in 1799**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: What was the rakhi system? → Protection offered to cultivators by the Sikhs in return for a tax of 20% of the produce.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing misl (Sikh band) with mansab (Mughal rank).
- Thinking Ranjit Singh founded the Khalsa — Guru Gobind Singh did in 1699.

scenes.text: In the hills of Maharashtra, Shivaji built a kingdom with the help of peasant-pastoralist warriors.
Mobile armies could raid far away and retreat to strong hill forts.
Under the Peshwas, Maratha power stretched from the Deccan to Rajasthan, Malwa and beyond.

steps.title: Shivaji (1627–1680)
steps.body: The Maratha kingdom was a regional kingdom that resisted Mughal rule. **Shivaji** carved out a stable kingdom with the support of powerful warrior families (**deshmukhs**). Groups of highly mobile, **peasant-pastoralists (kunbis)** provided the backbone of the army. Shivaji used these forces to challenge the Mughals in the peninsula.

steps.title: The Peshwas
steps.body: After Shivaji's death, effective power in the Maratha state was wielded by a family of Chitpavan Brahmanas who served his successors as **Peshwa** (principal minister). **Pune** became the capital. Under the Peshwas, the Marathas developed a very successful military organisation — bypassing fortified Mughal areas, raiding cities and engaging armies where supply lines could be disrupted. Between 1720 and 1761, the Maratha empire expanded: Malwa and Gujarat were seized from the Mughals by the 1730s; by the 1730s the Maratha king was recognised as overlord of the Deccan peninsula. They raided Rajasthan, Punjab, Bengal, Orissa, Karnataka and Tamil and Telugu areas.

steps.title: Chauth and sardeshmukhi
steps.body: The Marathas had the right to levy **chauth** — **25% of the land revenue** claimed by zamindars — and **sardeshmukhi** — **9–10% of the land revenue** paid to the head revenue collector in the Deccan. Expansion brought enormous resources but made other rulers hostile; they did not support the Marathas at the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)**. Within their domains, the Marathas encouraged agriculture, revived trade and developed new cities like Malwa's **Ujjain** (under Scindhia) and **Indore** (Holkar).

steps.title: The Jats
steps.body: Like other groups, the **Jats** consolidated their power in the late 17th and 18th centuries. Under **Churaman**, they acquired control over territories west of Delhi, and by the 1680s dominated the region between Delhi and Agra. The Jats were prosperous agriculturists; towns like **Panipat and Ballabhgarh** became important trading centres. Under **Suraj Mal**, the kingdom of **Bharatpur** emerged as a strong state.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Distinguish chauth and sardeshmukhi. → Chauth: 25% of land revenue claimed by zamindars. Sardeshmukhi: 9–10% paid to the head revenue collector.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the Peshwa the Maratha king — he was the principal minister.
- Mixing Jat leaders: Churaman (expansion), Suraj Mal (Bharatpur).

scenes.text: At a lakeside picnic, Riya notices rocks, water, the breeze and birds.
Her father says: "Land, water, air and living things — together they make our environment."
Each part depends on the others.

steps.title: What is environment?
steps.body: **Environment** is everything around us — the place, people, things and nature that surround a living organism. It is a combination of **natural** (land, water, air, plants, animals) and **human-made** (buildings, roads, parks, bridges, industries) things.

steps.title: Four domains
steps.body:
- **Lithosphere**: the solid crust or hard top layer of the Earth — rocks and minerals, covered by a thin layer of soil. Landforms: mountains, plateaus, plains, valleys. It gives forests, grasslands, agricultural land, human settlements and minerals.
- **Hydrosphere**: domain of water — rivers, lakes, seas, oceans, estuaries.
- **Atmosphere**: thin layer of air surrounding the Earth, held by gravity; protects us from the harmful rays and scorching heat of the Sun.
- **Biosphere**: the narrow zone where land, water and air interact and life exists — the plant kingdom and the animal kingdom.

steps.title: Solved example 2

- Forgetting humans are part of the biosphere.

scenes.text: In a small pond, fish eat insects, frogs eat insects, herons eat fish and frogs.
Water plants make food using sunlight; bacteria break down dead matter.
The pond is an ecosystem — living things and their surroundings working together.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: All plants, animals and human beings depend on their immediate surroundings and are often interrelated. A system formed by the interaction of all living organisms with each other and with the physical and chemical factors of the environment is an **ecosystem**.

steps.title: Examples and sizes
steps.body: Ecosystems can be large or small: a pond, a forest, a desert, grassland, an ocean, even a fish tank. In each, producers (plants), consumers (animals) and decomposers (bacteria, fungi) depend on one another and on sunlight, water, soil and air.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Give one example of interdependence in a forest ecosystem. → Trees give food and shelter to birds; birds disperse seeds of trees.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: What happens to a pond ecosystem if its water dries up? → Fish and water plants die; frogs and birds lose food and must move; the whole system collapses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking an ecosystem must be large — a pond is an ecosystem.
- Forgetting non-living parts (water, soil, sunlight).

scenes.text: Early humans lived in caves and depended on nature for food, shelter and clothing.
Later they learned to grow crops, domesticate animals and live in villages.
Today we build cities, roads and factories — changing the environment more than ever.

steps.title: Human environment
steps.body: Human beings interact with the environment and modify it according to their needs. Early humans adapted to nature. With time they learned new skills: grow crops, domesticate animals, lead a settled life; invented the wheel; practised barter; trade and commerce developed. The **Industrial Revolution** enabled large-scale production. Transportation became faster; the **information revolution** made communication easier and speedier across the world. Human-made environment: buildings, parks, bridges, roads, industries, monuments.

steps.title: Balance
steps.body: Rapid modification led to problems — pollution of air, water and land, deforestation, climate change. A **perfect balance** between the natural and human environment is needed. **World Environment Day** is observed on **5 June**. Humans must learn to live in harmony with the environment.

- **Human-made environment**: things built by people — buildings, roads, bridges, parks, industries, monuments.

questions.why: The biosphere is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet and interact to support life.

questions.q: Which is a natural component?
questions.why: A river is a natural part of the environment. Roads, bridges and factories are built by people.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A pond is an ecosystem. Reason (R): Organisms in a pond interact with each other and with water, light and soil.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: a pond is an ecosystem. R is true: its organisms interact with each other and with water, light and soil. That is the meaning of an ecosystem, so R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Human-made environment never affects the natural environment. Reason (R): Humans build roads and factories.
questions.why: A is false: roads and factories do affect nature, for example by clearing land and causing pollution. R is true that humans build them, but that does not support A.

questions.q: Which domain gives us minerals?
questions.why: The lithosphere is the Earth's solid crust, made of rocks and minerals, so it gives us minerals.

questions.q: Barter system means
questions.why: In the barter system people exchange goods or services directly, without using money.

questions.q: Case: A city cut its trees for a highway; summers became hotter and floods worse. What is missing?
options: Balance between human and natural environment
questions.why: Cutting the trees upset the natural environment and led to heat and floods. What was missing was a balance between development and nature.

questions.q: Case: A student sorts "hill, sea, wind, deer". Which domain is NOT represented?
questions.why: A hill is in the lithosphere, the sea in the hydrosphere, wind in the atmosphere and a deer in the biosphere. So all four domains are present.

questions.q: The information revolution mainly changed
questions.why: The information revolution changed how we communicate, making it faster through computers, the internet and phones.

questions.q: Why must decomposers be part of every ecosystem?
options: They recycle nutrients from dead matter
questions.why: Decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil. Without them, nutrients would not be recycled.

questions.q: Which shows interaction of all four domains?
options: A farmer growing crops using soil, rain, air and plants
questions.why: A farmer uses soil (lithosphere), rain (hydrosphere), air (atmosphere) and plants (biosphere). So all four domains interact in his work.

courses.title: Ch 2 · Inside Our Earth (Geography)
courses.summary: The layers of the Earth — crust, mantle and core — the three kinds of rocks and how they form, the rock cycle, and the minerals and uses of rocks.
outcomes: Learners can describe the layers of the Earth with their thickness and materials
Learners can distinguish igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks with examples
Learners can explain the rock cycle
Learners can describe uses of rocks and minerals

scenes.text: Peel an onion — layer under layer. The Earth is built in layers too.
The deepest mine in the world reaches only about 4 km; the Earth's centre is about 6000 km down.
Scientists study earthquakes and volcanoes to learn about the interior.

steps.title: Crust
steps.body:
The uppermost layer, the **crust**, is the thinnest. About **35 km** on continental masses and only **5 km** on the ocean floors.

- Continental crust: mainly **silica and alumina** → called **sial** (si = silica, al = alumina).
- Oceanic crust: mainly **silica and magnesium** → **sima** (si = silica, ma = magnesium).

steps.title: Mantle and core
steps.body:
- **Mantle**: just beneath the crust, extending to a depth of about **2900 km**.
- **Core**: innermost layer, radius about **3500 km**, mainly **nickel and iron** → **nife** (ni = nickel, fe = ferrous/iron). The central core has very high temperature and pressure.

steps.title: How deep have we gone?
steps.body: To reach the centre of the Earth (about 6000 km below the ocean floor) is impossible today; the deepest mine (in South Africa) is about 4 km deep, and oil drilling has gone about 6 km.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is the crust called sial on continents but sima under oceans? → Continental crust is rich in silica and alumina; oceanic crust in silica and magnesium.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Arrange the layers by depth from the surface. → Crust (~35 km on continents) → mantle (to ~2900 km) → core (radius ~3500 km).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping sial and sima.
- Thinking the crust is the thickest layer — it is the thinnest.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: Layer below the crust, to ~2900 km

quiz.why: Continental crust is about 35 km thick on average. Oceanic crust is only about 5 km thick.

quiz.q: The core is made mainly of
quiz.why: The Earth's core is made mainly of nickel and iron. It is sometimes called nife.
The mantle lies below the crust and extends to about 2900 km deep.
The crust is the thinnest layer, about 5 to 35 km. The mantle and core are much thicker.
Oceanic crust is thinner than continental crust, only about 5 km thick.

scenes.text: Arjun collects three rocks: a speckled granite, a layered sandstone and a shiny marble.
His teacher explains: one formed from molten lava, one from layers of sand, one changed by heat and pressure.
Every rock tells the story of how it was made.

steps.title: Rocks and minerals
steps.body: Any natural mass of mineral matter that makes up the Earth's crust is a **rock**. Rocks can be of different colour, size and texture. There are three major types.

steps.title: Igneous rocks
steps.body:
When molten **magma** cools, it becomes solid — **igneous rocks** (primary rocks).

- **Extrusive igneous**: molten lava comes onto the surface and cools rapidly → very fine grains. **Basalt** (Deccan plateau is made of basalt).
- **Intrusive igneous**: molten magma cools deep inside the crust slowly → large grains. **Granite** (used for grinding stones).

steps.title: Sedimentary and metamorphic
steps.body:
- **Sedimentary rocks**: rocks roll down, crack, break into small fragments (**sediments**); these are transported and deposited by wind, water etc. Loose sediments get compressed and hardened in layers. Example: **sandstone** (from grains of sand). They may contain **fossils** of plants, animals and micro-organisms.
- **Metamorphic rocks**: igneous and sedimentary rocks change into metamorphic rocks under **great heat and pressure**. **Clay → slate**, **limestone → marble**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why does granite have large grains and basalt fine grains? → Granite cools slowly deep inside the Earth; basalt cools quickly on the surface.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Classify: marble, basalt, sandstone, slate, granite → metamorphic, igneous (extrusive), sedimentary, metamorphic, igneous (intrusive).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling marble sedimentary — it is metamorphic (from limestone).
- Thinking fossils are found in igneous rocks; they are mostly in sedimentary rocks.

activity.prompt: Classify the rock.

quiz.why: Igneous rocks form when molten magma or lava cools and hardens. They are called primary rocks.
The Deccan plateau is made mainly of basalt, from lava that flowed out and cooled long ago.
Heat and pressure change limestone into marble. This process is called metamorphism.
Clay changes to slate under heat and pressure, so slate is a metamorphic rock.
Fossils are mostly found in sedimentary rocks, because soft layers of sediment can bury remains. Igneous rocks form from hot lava, which destroys remains.

lessons.title: The rock cycle, minerals and uses

scenes.text: Lava cools into basalt. Rain and wind wear it into sand.
Rivers carry the sand to the sea where it hardens into sandstone.
Deep inside, heat turns it into new rock, which may melt into magma again.

steps.title: Rock cycle
steps.body: Rocks change from one type to another in a cycle: molten magma cools → **igneous** rocks; broken into particles → **sedimentary** rocks; under heat and pressure → **metamorphic** rocks; under great heat and pressure, metamorphic rocks may melt into magma again. This transformation of one type of rock into another under certain conditions in a cyclic manner is the **rock cycle**.

steps.title: Minerals and uses
steps.body:
Rocks are made of **minerals** — naturally occurring substances with certain physical properties and definite chemical composition. Minerals are important: some are used as fuels — **coal, natural gas, petroleum**; others in industries — **iron, aluminium, gold, uranium**; in medicine, fertilisers etc.

Rocks are useful for roads, houses and buildings; stones are used in games (seven stones/pithoo, hopscotch, five stones).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Trace a path in the rock cycle from igneous to metamorphic. → Igneous → weathered into sediments → sedimentary rock → heat and pressure → metamorphic.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Name two minerals used as fuel and two used in industry. → Coal, petroleum; iron, aluminium.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the rock cycle has only one direction — rocks can change in several ways.
- Confusing rocks (mixtures) with minerals (definite composition).

activity.prompt: Arrange one path of the rock cycle.
items: Magma cools to form igneous rock
Sediments are compressed into sedimentary rock
Heat and pressure form metamorphic rock

options: transformation of rocks from one type to another
quiz.why: The rock cycle is the process by which rocks change from one type to another. For example, igneous rock can become sedimentary or metamorphic and then melt into magma.
A mineral is a natural substance with a definite chemical composition and set properties.
Coal is a mineral fuel, used to produce energy. Iron and gold are metals used otherwise.
Rocks are made up of one or more minerals.

quiz.q: Metamorphic rocks can melt to form
quiz.why: Metamorphic rocks may melt to form magma, which can cool and form new igneous rocks. This continues the cycle.

- Saying all hard rocks are igneous.

quiz.why: The Taj Mahal is made of white marble, a metamorphic rock.

quiz.q: Red Fort is built mainly of
quiz.why: The Red Fort is built mainly of red sandstone, a sedimentary rock.
The mantle is the middle layer of the Earth, between the crust and the core.
Fossils are commonly found in sedimentary rocks, which form in layers from sediments.
Granite is very hard, so it is used for grinding stones and kitchen counters. Chalk, glass and paper are made from other materials.

questions.q: Outermost layer of the Earth
questions.why: The crust is the outermost layer of the Earth. Below it are the mantle and then the core.

questions.q: Core is mainly
questions.why: The core is mainly nickel and iron, which is why it is called nife.

questions.q: Granite is an
questions.why: Granite forms when magma cools slowly deep inside the Earth, so it is an intrusive igneous rock. It has large crystals.

questions.q: Marble is formed from
questions.why: Marble forms from limestone when it is changed by heat and pressure (metamorphism).

questions.q: Sima stands for
questions.why: Sima stands for silica and magnesium. It is the main material of the oceanic crust.

questions.q: Sedimentary rocks form from
questions.why: Sedimentary rocks form when layers of sediments are pressed and cemented together over a long time.

questions.q: Radius of the core (approx.)
questions.why: The core has a radius of about 3500 km. The mantle is about 2900 km thick.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Basalt has fine grains. Reason (R): Lava cools rapidly on the surface.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: basalt has fine grains. R is true: lava cools rapidly on the surface, so crystals have no time to grow big. R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The crust is the thickest layer of the Earth. Reason (R): It forms the ocean floor and continents.
questions.why: A is false: the crust is the thinnest layer, not the thickest. R is true that it forms the continents and the ocean floor.

questions.q: Slate forms from
questions.why: Slate forms from clay, changed by heat and pressure. It is a metamorphic rock.

questions.q: Fossils help us learn about
questions.why: Fossils are the remains of plants and animals of the past, so they tell us about past life.

questions.q: Case: A geologist finds a layered rock with shells of sea creatures high in the Himalayas. The rock is likely
questions.why: Layers and fossils point to a sedimentary rock. Layers of sediment buried the sea creatures long ago, and the rock was later lifted high.

questions.q: Case: A rock cooled deep underground and was later exposed by erosion. It has large crystals. Likely
questions.why: Rock that cooled slowly underground has large crystals, which suggests an intrusive igneous rock like granite. Basalt cools quickly on the surface and has fine grains.

questions.q: Why can't we drill to the Earth's centre?
options: Extreme heat and pressure; it is about 6000 km deep
questions.why: The Earth's centre is about 6000 km deep, and the heat and pressure rise greatly with depth. The deepest mines go only a few kilometres.

questions.q: Which sequence is a possible rock cycle path?
questions.why: Sedimentary rock can change to metamorphic rock, which can melt to magma, and magma cools to igneous rock. This is a possible path in the rock cycle. The others include air, water and the core, which are not rock types.

questions.q: Which layer is described as "nife" and why?
questions.why: Nife stands for nickel and iron, the main substances of the core.

courses.title: Ch 3 · Our Changing Earth (Geography)
courses.summary: Moving lithospheric plates, earthquakes and volcanoes, and the landforms created by rivers, sea waves, glaciers and wind through weathering and erosion — with earthquake safety tips.
outcomes: Learners can explain endogenic and exogenic forces and plate movement
Learners can describe earthquakes, their measurement and safety measures
Learners can describe landforms made by rivers, sea waves, ice and wind
Learners can distinguish weathering and erosion

scenes.text: During class, the desks begin to rattle and the fan swings.
The teacher calls: "Drop, cover, hold!" Everyone ducks under their desks.
Later they learn that the ground shook because huge plates of rock moved deep below.

steps.title: Lithospheric plates and forces
steps.body:
The lithosphere is broken into a number of plates called **lithospheric plates**, which move around very slowly — just a few millimetres each year — because of the movement of molten magma inside the Earth.

- **Endogenic forces**: act in the interior of the Earth (cause earthquakes, volcanoes).
- **Exogenic forces**: work on the surface (weathering, erosion, deposition).

steps.title: Earthquakes
steps.body: When lithospheric plates move, the surface vibrates — an **earthquake**. The place in the crust where the movement starts is the **focus**; the place on the surface above the focus is the **epicentre**. Vibrations travel outwards from the epicentre as waves; greatest damage is usually closest to the epicentre. Earthquakes are measured with a **seismograph**; magnitude on the **Richter scale** (2.0 or less – little felt; above 5.0 – damage from falling objects; 6.0 or more – very strong; 7.0 and above – major earthquake). Common predictions include animal behaviour.

steps.title: Volcanoes
steps.body: A **volcano** is a vent (opening) in the Earth's crust through which molten material (lava, ash, gases) erupts suddenly.

steps.title: Earthquake safety
steps.body:
- Indoors: **drop, cover and hold** under a sturdy table; stay away from windows, mirrors, heavy furniture.
- Outdoors: move to an open area away from buildings, trees, power lines.
- Do not use lifts. Afterwards, check for injuries; call **112** in emergencies.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Distinguish focus and epicentre. → Focus: place inside the crust where movement starts. Epicentre: point on the surface directly above the focus.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking plates move fast; they move only millimetres a year.
- Running outside during shaking from a high floor — it is safer to drop, cover and hold.

activity.prompt: Match the term with its meaning.
pairs: Starting point of an earthquake inside the crust
Point on the surface above the focus
Force acting on the Earth's surface
Vent through which molten material erupts

quiz.why: Earthquakes are measured on the Richter scale, which gives their magnitude.

quiz.q: Point on the surface above the focus
quiz.why: The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus, where the earthquake starts underground.
The plates move very slowly, only a few millimetres a year.
Forces working inside the Earth are called endogenic forces. Forces on the surface are exogenic.

quiz.q: During an earthquake indoors, you should
quiz.why: Indoors during an earthquake, drop to the ground, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on. Stay away from windows, and do not use the lift.

scenes.text: High in the mountains a river rushes down steep slopes, cutting deep valleys.
Where it falls over a hard rock edge, it forms a waterfall.
Down in the plains it winds in loops, floods its banks and finally splits into many streams near the sea.

steps.title: Weathering and erosion
steps.body:
- **Weathering**: breaking up of rocks on the Earth's surface.
- **Erosion**: wearing away of the landscape by agents like **water, wind and ice**. The eroded material is carried away and **deposited** elsewhere. These processes create various landforms.

steps.title: River landforms
steps.body:
- **Waterfall**: river falls over a steep hard rock or a steep valley side. **Angel Falls of Venezuela** is the highest waterfall in the world.
- **Meanders**: as the river enters the plain, it twists and turns forming large bends.
- **Ox-bow lake**: erosion and deposition cut off a meander loop, forming a lake.
- **Floodplains**: when a river overflows, it deposits fine soil and sediments on the banks — fertile flat land.
- **Levees**: raised banks formed by deposition.
- **Distributaries and delta**: near the sea the river splits into many streams (distributaries); the mouth gets a deposit called a **delta**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: How is an ox-bow lake formed? → A meander loop grows; erosion and deposition at its ends cut it off from the main river, leaving a curved lake.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why are floodplains good for farming? → Floods deposit fertile soil and sediment on them.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing weathering (breaking of rocks in place) and erosion (wearing away and carrying).
- Thinking a delta forms in the mountains — it forms at the river mouth.

activity.prompt: Arrange river landforms from the mountains to the sea.
items: V-shaped valley and waterfall in the hills
Ox-bow lake from a cut-off meander
Distributaries and delta at the mouth

quiz.why: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the world's highest waterfall.
Large bends in a river's course are called meanders.
When a meander gets cut off from the main river, it becomes an ox-bow lake.
During floods a river deposits sediment along its banks, building raised banks called levees.

quiz.q: Breaking up of rocks on the surface
quiz.why: Weathering is the breaking up of rocks on the Earth's surface. Erosion carries the material away.

lessons.title: Work of sea waves, ice and wind

scenes.text: On a rocky coast, waves have carved caves, arches and lonely pillars of rock.
In the Himalayas, slow rivers of ice grind valleys and leave piles of rocks.
In the desert, the wind has shaped a rock like a giant mushroom.

steps.title: Sea waves
steps.body: Waves strike rocks continuously; cracks develop and become larger, forming hollow **sea caves**. As cavities become bigger, only the roof remains — **sea arches**. Further erosion breaks the roof and only walls are left — **stacks**. The steep rocky coast rising almost vertically above sea water is a **sea cliff**. Waves deposit sediments along shores, forming **beaches**.

steps.title: Ice (glaciers)
steps.body: **Glaciers** are 'rivers' of ice which erode the landscape by bulldozing soil and stones to expose solid rock below; they carve out deep hollows that fill with water and become beautiful lakes in the mountains. Material carried by the glacier — rocks big and small, sand and silt — gets deposited, forming **glacial moraines**.

steps.title: Wind
steps.body: Wind is an active agent of erosion and deposition in deserts. It erodes the lower section of rocks more than the upper part, forming **mushroom rocks** (narrow base, wider top). When wind blows, it lifts and transports sand; when it stops, sand falls and gets deposited in low hill-like structures — **sand dunes**. When grains of sand are very fine and light, wind carries them over long distances; deposited over large areas they form **loess** (large deposits are found in **China**).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Arrange the sequence of coastal erosion. → Sea cave → sea arch → stack.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Why do mushroom rocks have a narrow base? → Wind carries sand close to the ground, which erodes the lower part more than the top.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing stacks (erosion) with beaches (deposition).
- Mixing moraines (glacier) and loess (wind).

activity.prompt: Which agent made it?

quiz.why: When the roof of a sea arch collapses, the pillar of rock left standing in the sea is a stack.
Rocks and soil deposited by a glacier are called moraines.
Wind erosion in deserts shapes rocks into mushroom forms, called mushroom rocks.

quiz.q: Large deposits of loess are found in
quiz.why: Loess, a fine wind-blown deposit, is found in large amounts in China.
Sea waves deposit sand and pebbles along the shore, forming beaches.

For each, students name the landform and the agent that made it.

steps.title: Quick guide
steps.body:
- Rivers: waterfall, meander, ox-bow lake, floodplain, levee, delta
- Sea waves: sea cave, arch, stack, cliff, beach
- Glaciers: glacial lakes, moraines
- Wind: mushroom rock, sand dune, loess

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: A curved lake next to a winding river → **ox-bow lake**, made by the river (erosion + deposition).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: A pillar of rock standing in the sea near the coast → **stack**, made by sea waves after an arch collapsed.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Calling every hill of sand a 'mountain' — sand hills are dunes.
- Thinking moraines are made by rivers.

quiz.q: A lake left by a cut-off river bend
quiz.why: A meander that gets cut off from the river leaves an ox-bow lake.
A stack is a pillar of rock left standing in the sea after waves wear away the rest.

quiz.q: Heap of rocks deposited by a glacier
quiz.why: A moraine is a heap of rocks and soil deposited by a glacier.
Loess is fine, wind-blown dust that settles as deposits.
Waves erode rock at the coast and leave a steep rocky face, called a sea cliff.

questions.q: Instrument that records earthquakes
questions.why: A seismograph records the waves of an earthquake. A barometer measures air pressure.

questions.q: Mushroom rocks are made by
questions.why: Wind erosion in deserts wears rocks into mushroom shapes. So mushroom rocks are made by wind.

questions.q: Highest waterfall
questions.why: Angel Falls in Venezuela is the highest waterfall in the world.

questions.q: Point inside the crust where an earthquake begins
questions.why: The focus is the point inside the crust where the earthquake starts. The epicentre is the point above it on the surface.

questions.q: Wearing away of land by water, wind, ice
questions.why: Erosion is the wearing away of land by running water, wind or ice. Weathering is the breaking of rock in place.

questions.q: Ox-bow lakes form in
questions.why: Ox-bow lakes form on plains where a river forms meanders that are later cut off.

questions.q: Earthquake of magnitude 7 or more is
questions.why: On the Richter scale an earthquake of magnitude 7 or more is major and can cause heavy damage.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Floodplains are fertile. Reason (R): Rivers deposit fine soil during floods.
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: floodplains are fertile. R is true: rivers deposit fine soil during floods, which adds nutrients. So R explains A.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Weathering and erosion are the same. Reason (R): Both are exogenic processes.
questions.why: A is false: weathering breaks rock down in place, whereas erosion carries it away. R is true that both are exogenic processes, but this does not make them the same.

questions.q: Correct order of coastal erosion
questions.why: Waves first carve a cave in a cliff. The cave widens into an arch, and when the arch's roof falls, a stack is left.

questions.q: Delta forms at the
questions.why: A delta forms at the mouth of a river, where the river slows down, drops its sediment and splits into branches before entering the sea.

questions.q: Case: A village near a river floods every year but has rich crops. The village is likely on a
questions.why: Floods leave fine, fertile silt on the land beside a river. So a village that floods yearly but has rich crops is likely on a floodplain.

questions.q: Case: During an earthquake, Ravi is on the 5th floor. Best action?
options: Drop under a sturdy table and hold on
questions.why: In an earthquake, drop down, take cover under a sturdy table and hold on until the shaking stops. Lifts, balconies and windows are dangerous.

questions.q: Which pair is correct?
questions.why: A glacier carries and deposits rocks and soil as moraines. Levees come from rivers, loess from wind and stacks from sea waves, so the other pairs are mismatched.

questions.q: Why are earthquakes most damaging near the epicentre?
options: Waves are strongest closest to it
questions.why: Earthquake waves lose energy as they spread out. So the shaking is strongest, and damage greatest, closest to the epicentre.

questions.q: Lithospheric plates move because of
options: movement of molten magma inside the Earth
questions.why: The lithospheric plates float on hot, molten magma in the mantle, and the slow movement of this magma makes them move. This is an endogenic cause.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Air (Geography)
courses.summary: The composition and layers of the atmosphere, weather and climate, temperature and insolation, air pressure and winds, moisture, humidity and kinds of rainfall.
outcomes: Learners can state the composition of air and the role of each gas
Learners can describe the five layers of the atmosphere
Learners can distinguish weather and climate and explain temperature and pressure
Learners can classify winds and types of rainfall

scenes.text: Astronaut photos show Earth wrapped in a thin blue haze.
That haze is the atmosphere — the air that lets us breathe and keeps us warm.
Mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with small amounts of other gases.

steps.title: Gases in air
steps.body:
Our Earth is surrounded by a huge blanket of air called the **atmosphere**. Air is a mixture of many gases:

- **Nitrogen ≈ 78%**
- **Oxygen ≈ 21%**
- **Argon ≈ 0.93%**
- **Carbon dioxide ≈ 0.03%**
- Others (helium, ozone, hydrogen, etc.) in tiny amounts

Air also contains water vapour and dust particles.

steps.title: Role of the gases
steps.body:
- **Nitrogen**: plants need it but cannot take it directly from air; bacteria in soil and roots of some plants change it into a usable form.
- **Oxygen**: breathed by humans and animals; plants produce it in photosynthesis.
- **Carbon dioxide**: plants use it to make food; it absorbs heat radiated by the Earth, keeping the planet warm. But burning fuels adds more CO₂, increasing heat in the atmosphere — the **greenhouse effect** — leading to **global warming**.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why is CO₂ important even though it is only about 0.03% of air? → Plants need it for photosynthesis, and it keeps the Earth warm by absorbing heat.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: How do plants get nitrogen? → Bacteria in soil and in roots of some plants convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying oxygen is the most abundant gas — it is nitrogen.
- Thinking the greenhouse effect is always bad — some is needed to keep Earth warm; extra CO₂ causes global warming.

activity.prompt: Match the gas to its share or role.
pairs: Small amount; absorbs harmful UV rays

quiz.why: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of air. Oxygen is about 21%, and the rest is argon, carbon dioxide and other gases.
Oxygen is about 21% of the air. Nitrogen is the largest part at 78%.

quiz.q: Gas used by plants to make food
quiz.why: Plants take in carbon dioxide and use it in photosynthesis to make food. Argon and helium are not used.
More CO₂ traps more heat in the air, which is the greenhouse effect. This leads to global warming.
Plants cannot use nitrogen directly from the air. Bacteria in the soil and root nodules change it into a form plants can take up, called nitrogen fixation.

scenes.text: A jet plane cruises above the clouds where the air is calm.
Higher up, meteors burn up as streaks of light.
Even higher, radio waves bounce off a charged layer back to Earth.

steps.title: Five layers
steps.body:
Starting from the Earth's surface:

1. **Troposphere** (average height ~13 km): most important layer — air we breathe; almost all weather (rain, fog, hailstorms) occurs here.
2. **Stratosphere** (up to ~50 km): almost free from clouds and weather, so ideal for **flying aeroplanes**; contains the **ozone layer**, which protects us from harmful UV rays.
3. **Mesosphere** (up to ~80 km): **meteorites burn up** here on entering from space.
4. **Thermosphere** (80–400 km): temperature rises very rapidly with height; the **ionosphere** is part of it — helps radio transmission (radio waves sent from Earth are reflected back).
5. **Exosphere**: uppermost layer with very thin air; light gases like helium and hydrogen float into space from here.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why do aeroplanes fly in the stratosphere? → It is almost free from clouds and weather disturbances.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: In which layer do we live and where does weather occur? → **Troposphere**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting the ozone layer in the troposphere — it is in the stratosphere.
- Mixing mesosphere (meteors burn) and thermosphere (ionosphere).

"Mumbai gets heavy rain every monsoon" — that is climate.
Weather can change hour by hour; climate is the average over many years.

steps.title: Weather and climate
steps.body: **Weather** is the hour-to-hour, day-to-day condition of the atmosphere; it can change dramatically. The average weather condition of a place over a long period is its **climate**. Elements: temperature, pressure, wind, moisture, rainfall.

steps.title: Temperature and insolation
steps.body: The degree of hotness and coldness of air is **temperature**. It changes between day and night and from season to season. An important factor is **insolation** — incoming solar energy intercepted by the Earth. Insolation decreases from the **equator towards the poles**, so temperature too. Temperatures in cities are higher than in villages (concrete and metal absorb heat; less vegetation).

steps.title: Air pressure
steps.body:
**Air pressure** is the pressure exerted by the weight of air on the Earth's surface. It is highest at sea level and **decreases with height**. Horizontally, it depends on temperature:

- Where temperature is **high**, air heats up and rises → **low pressure** → cloudy skies and wet weather.
- Where temperature is **low**, air is cold and heavy, it sinks → **high pressure** → clear and sunny skies.

**Air always moves from high pressure to low pressure areas.**

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why do mountaineers carry oxygen cylinders? → Air pressure and the amount of oxygen decrease with height, making breathing difficult.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: An area has low pressure. Expect what weather? → Rising air, cloudy and wet weather.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping weather (short-term) and climate (long-term).
- Thinking air moves from low to high pressure — it moves from high to low.

Winds carry moisture; when moist air rises and cools, it rains.

steps.title: Winds
steps.body:
The movement of air from high pressure to low pressure is **wind**.

- **Permanent winds**: blow constantly in a particular direction throughout the year — **trade winds, westerlies, easterlies**.
- **Seasonal winds**: change direction with seasons — **monsoon** winds in India.
- **Local winds**: blow only during a particular period of the day or year in a small area — land and sea breezes; the hot, dry **loo** of the northern plains of India.

steps.title: Moisture and humidity
steps.body: When water evaporates from land and water bodies, it becomes water vapour. **Moisture** in the air at any time is **humidity**. When air is full of water vapour, it is humid; on a humid day, clothes take longer to dry and sweat does not evaporate easily. When water vapour rises, it cools and condenses into tiny droplets — **clouds**. When droplets become too heavy, they fall as **precipitation** (rain, snow, sleet).

steps.title: Types of rainfall
steps.body:
- **Convectional rainfall**: heated air rises, cools and forms clouds — common in hot, equatorial regions (afternoon rain).
- **Orographic (relief) rainfall**: moist air is forced to rise along a mountain; the windward side gets heavy rain, the other side (rain-shadow) stays dry.
- **Cyclonic rainfall**: associated with cyclones.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Q: Why does the windward side of the Western Ghats get heavy rain and the leeward side less? → Moist monsoon winds rise along the slope, cool and shed rain (orographic); descending air on the other side is dry.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Q: Classify the monsoon: permanent, seasonal or local? → **Seasonal**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the loo a permanent wind — it is local.
- Thinking humidity is the same as rainfall.
